speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE ON THE PACIFIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I take advantage of this moment to correct a false impression that seems to exist in regard to the use of Japanese coal by the Canadian Government Merchant Marine on the Pacific. The impression seems to have got abroad, that the Government Merchant Marine intend to use Japanese coal, or are bringing Japanese coal to this country. The matter came up some time ago in connection with a question asked by an hon. member, and a reply was given at the time that the coal that came from Japan was merely in the nature of ballast; it was cheaper to the company at the time to purchase coal for that purpose than to purchase ballast in some other form. I understand that recently the matter has come up again, and some fear is expressed on the part of certain hon. members from the West that the Government Merchant Marine intend to adopt as a policy the bringing of coal from Japan to Canada. Hon. members know that the Merchant Marine is under the Board of Directors of the National Railways. The Government has not to do with the control of its affairs, or the operation of its steamers; but in answering the question that was asked some little time ago the following statement was made:
As far as they can possibly do so the steamers of the -Government Merchant Marine will hereafter use onily British Columbia coal on the Pacific ocean.
That statement was given to the Government by the Board of Directors of the National Railways and, as I understand it,

The Budget-Mr. Bristol
indicates its policy then and its policy at '-he present time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, June, 1, the debate on the motion of Hon. W. S. Fielding (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Ways and Means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Hon. Sir Henry Drayton.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join with
other members of the House in congratulating the Minister of Finance upon the manner in which he delivered this-his sixteenth budget speech. I do not believe that there is any man in Canada better equipped, by long experience and by ability, to present that speech; and I do not suppose that the Finance Minister, well informed as he is, was ever confronted by a more difficult situation, because he has to satisfy everybody on his own side of the House, from the free trader in the person of my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) to the ultra-protectionist, my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Raymond). Anybody who can do that is certainly something of a magician as well as an able finance minister. Now my hon. friend had a great many difficulties to encounter, and I have no doubt that if those difficulties were not so numerous he would have presented a budget more on the lines of his budget of 1907 rather than the class of budget which he brought down recently. But the criticism that I would offer in respect to the budget as a budget is, that substantially it does nothing for the stimulation or promotion of Canadian trade or Canadian agriculture. It is" what you might call a " safety first " or " stand pat " budget. Whatever reductions or changes have been made are for the benefit of our business competitors the United States, Great Britain, and particularly Germany. Now, everybody in this House knows that, since the war, every civilized country has been doing everything it possibly could to protect, preserve and maintain the home market of that country for its own people and to protect and maintain its own home industries. I suppose the two most conspicuous examples with which we are familiar are Great Britain and the United States of America, and I would have thought that under those circumstances, a Finance Minister of the wide experience and great ability of the present occupant of that office would have taken into account the necessity in this country of not merely preserving matters in statu quo, but of doing what he reasonably could, so far as the tariff will do it, to promote, advance and protect the industries already existing in this country, to bring in other industries, and to give the people who have money to invest in industries a confidence that, so far as Canada is concerned, the policy which has been in force practically from 1879 to the present time is to be maintained unimpaired, and that the small modicum of protection given to our industries is not to be whittled away for the benefit of our American, English and German competitors.
I am going, first of all, to take up the case of Germany, because that is the most flagrant case, and I am rather inclined to think, from the way the minister spoke, that his mind is open to conviction, and if I can help him in any way to come to a conviction which will protect Canadian labour against the cheap and efficient labour of Germany, I think something of advantage will be done. What is the position in Germany as regards the wages paid to labour? It is well known-and the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) stated- that the value of a German mark to-day is a third of a cent. The latest information I can get from Germany is that skilled labour is paid 60 cents a day, and ordinary unskilled labour is paid 30 cents a day. But we will take sources perhaps more authentic, or, at least, more to be relied upon. I take Industrial and Labour Information, Volume II, No. 6, of 12th May, 1922, published at Geneva, by the Inter-
The Budget-Mr. Bristol

national Labour Office, and I find the following item:
It appears that the highest wages were paid in Hagen, dyers, 639 marks ($2.13) per week; belt makers, 650 marks ($2.17) per week; ribbon makers 654 marks ($2.18) per week, Essen and Hamburg, and the lowest in Bautzen (353 to 508 marks ($1,18 to $1.69) and Munich (409 to 624 marks ($1.37 to $175)).
The memorandum states that in most cases the weekly wages were lower than the minimum cost of living of a family of two adults and two children. In Berlin, for instance, the weekly minimum cost of living in December 1921, amounted to 557 marks ($1.86) per week, while in the same month the average wages in certain occupations were as follows: Printers (married), 553 marks per week ($1.84), railway mechanics, 418 marks ($1.40) ; railway labourers, 379 marks ($1.27) ; bricklayers, 552 marks ($1.84) ; building labourers, 522 marks ($1.74) ; navvies, 381 marks ($1.27). In Hamburg, the wage of bricklayers, 620 marks ($2.07), building labourers, 594 marks ($1.98), and navvies, 589 marks ($1.97) were in excess of the minimum cost of living, while those of joiners, 561 marks ($1.87).
I am not suggesting these figures for Government employees in Canada, but I find in the Frankfurter Zeitung, of 28th March, 1922, that they paid their Government officials the munificent salary of 11,000 marks per annum, or $36.67 for the lowest group, and for the highest group, No. 12, a salary of 40,000 marks, equal in Canadian funds to $133.34 per annum. It is not necessary for me to tell this House that the German mechanic is as well equipped for his work as any mechanic in the world, and they are not working six or eight hours a day; they are working all they can-ten hours a day, and an extra two hours for the Fatherland. The present tariff brought in by the hon. Minister of Finance takes for the valuation of German goods their fair market value in the country of production-Germany.	You can figure
what this value in Germany would be. Labour is 50 per cent of the cost of producing an article and then we have the raw material. I have shown you the labour cost, which is a prevailing cost. It practically means that the Germans can produce everything that is produced by factories in this country for about one tenth of our cost, and the freight rates from Germany to Canada are cheap. That is the real situation. Let me show you what Germany exported to Canada and the kind and character of the merchandise sold by that country to Canada in 1913. I thought it proper to read this list of articles to the House to show that, as far as competition with Germany is concerned, our mechanics have not only no protection, but there is practically nothing that is manufactured in this country, or that can be manufactured under reasonable competitive conditions, that Germany cannot today put on the Canadian market under the present tariff and easily undersell its Canadian competitors. It would be interesting to see, in this regard, what Great Britain has done to protect her industries-England, that free trade country that was once the proud boast of my hon. friends on the left. The British people are pretty level headed, when the question becomes one of real competition. They have passed what they call the Safeguarding of Industries Act. It reads, in part, as follows:
1.	If, on complaint being made to the board to that effect, it appears to the board that goods of any class or description (other than articles of food or drink) manufactured in a country outside the United Kingdom are being sold or offered for saile in the United Kingdom-
(b) At prices which by reason of depreciation in the value in relation to sterling of the currency of the country in which the goods are manufactured are below the prices at which similar goods can be profitably manufactured in the United Kingdom; and that by reason thereof employment in any industry in the United Kingdom is being or is likely to be seriously affected, the board may refer the matter for inquiry to a committee constituted for the purpose of this part of this act.
2.	If the committee report that as respects goods of any class or description manufactured in any country the conditions aforesaid are fulfilled the board may by order apply this part of this Act to goods of that class or description if manufactured in that country:
They go on -to state that where this is found, the customs duty, in addition to the ordinary duty,-shall be a customs duty equal to one-third of the value of the goods -in England, not in Germany. If England has to do this, what about poor Canada? Let us go on and see what the United States have done. They have not completed their legislation in this regard.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I only want to say to
my hon. friend that he is not asking a question except by way of making a long statement. Of course, there are people who will object to this act just as, if the Minister of Finance imposed a duty on German goods of one-third of the value in Canada of similar goods there would be people who would object to it. I have no doubt that in free trade England many people are agitating against the act, but I do not happen to know about that. If the hon. gentleman has information of that kind, he will have an opportunity of presenting it to the House. I am only pointing out. that such an act Is in force in England, and that it has not yet been repealed. This shows that British industry, in a country which has been free trade from 1846 to the present time, is so much alive to the situation and the necessity of protection against German goods that the British authorities are protecting, not merely industries that are at present in existence, but industries that anight be brought into existence and that might be injuriously affected. I will come back to this matter later on.
I want now to deal with the situation in the United States, because it is just as well to see what is done by our neighbours, although some of us may think they are foolish. No group of farmers in the civilized world, except the farmers of western Canada, is arguing in favour of free trade. The farmers of western Canada may be right in their views,-possibly but not probably;-honestly I have my doubts.
The Budget-Mr. Bristol

This is the bill as it is before the United States Congress at the present time. Let me cite section 315 of the new United States Tariff Act of 1922,-and in my humble judgment this is useful as showing the proper view of protection, which may be up or which may be down, but which is real only whe^i it fairly protects industries essential to the development of the country giving them such protection as will put them on a fairly even footing with their competitors in other countries. lit gives a smaller country an opportunity to develop its industries in competition with more powerful rivals. Section 315, to which I have referred, reads:
(a)	That in order to regulate the foreign commerce of the United States and to put into force and effect the policy of the Congress by this Act intended, whenever the President, upon investigation of the differences in conditions of competition in trade in the markets oif the United 'States of articles wholly or in part the growth or product of the United States and of Hike or similar articles wholly or in part the growth or product of competing foreign countries, shall find it thereby shown that the duties fixed in this Act do not equalize the said differences in conditions of competition in trade-
That is the aim of proper protection, namely, to give the people of the country a return for their money when they invest their capital, and to give the labourers a fair chance to get a fair day's pay for a fair day's work.
-he shall, by such investigation, ascertain said differences and determine and proclaim the changes in classifications or forms of duty or increases or decreases in any rate of duty provided in this Act shown by said ascertained differences in conditions of competition in trade necessary to equalize the same in the markets of the United 'States; that thirty days after the date of such proclamation or proclamations such changes in classification or in forms of duty shall take effect and such increased or decreased duties be levied, cofllected, and paid on such merchandise when imported directly or otherwise from the country of origin inito the United States: Provided, That until further provided by law the total increase or decrease of such rates of duty shall not exceed 50 per centum of the rates specified in this Act, or in any amendatory Act.
The next clause is a very interesting one:
(b)	That in order to regulate the foreign commerce of the United States and to put into force and effect the policy of the Congress by this act intended, whenever the President, upon investigation of the differences in conditions of competition in trade, in the markets of the United States, of articles wholly or in part the growth or product of the United States and of like or similar articQes wholly or in part the growth or product of competing foreign countries, shall find it thereby shown, that an

industry in the United States is being or likely to be materially injured by reason of the importation into the United States of foreign merchandise, and shall find it thereby shown that the value as determined under the provisions of paragraphs (1), (2), or (3) of subdivision (a) of section 402 of this act, is not a certain basis for the assessment of the particular duties, he shall make such findings public, together with a description of the class or kind of merchandise to which they apply in such detail as he may deem necessary for the guidance of appraising officers; that in such cases and upon the proclamation by the President becoming effective the ad valorem duty or duty based in whole or in part upon the value of the imported article in the country of exportation shall thereafter be based upon the American selling price,-
The duty is not based upon the value of the article in the country from which it comes, as such an article is being valued by our new tariff.
-as defined in subdivision (f) of section 402 of this act, of any similar competitive article manufactured or produced in the United States embraced within the class or kind of imported merchandise upon which the President has made public such a finding and proclamation.
I most respectfully submit that it would be wise for the Minister of Finance to reconsider this question in regard to German goods, and to provide that the ad valorem duty or duty based in whole or in part upon the value of the imported German article in the country of exportation shall thereafter be based upon the Canadian selling price of any similar competitive article manufactured or produced in Canada. There are various other provisions in the act showing that the United States is looking after its own interests from every angle. For instance, section 316 of the act reads:
That unfair methods of competition and unfair acts in the importation of merchandise into the United States, or in its sale by the owner, importer, consignee, or agent of either, the effect or tendency of which is to destroy or substantially injure an industry, efficiently and economically operated, in the United States, or to prevent the establishment of such an industry-
You will note how far it goes.
-or to restrain or monopolize trade and commerce in the United States, are hereby declared unlawful, and when found by the President to exist shall be dealt with, in addition to any other provisions of law, as hereinafter provided.
So much for the United States. Now, I would call the attention of the House to the fact, if it is necessary to labour the point further, that France, on the 28th of March, 1921, increased the maximum rates of duty, making the maximum rate exceed the minimum rate in varying proportions,

The Budget-Mr. Bristol
not exceeding 300 per cent, whereas formerly the difference between these rates was 100 per cent. The preamble to the decree explained that the measure is one of the results of the investigation which has been made of the steps which need to be taken in order to safeguard French industries, the very existence of which is threatened by the competition of goods from countries with depreciated exchange.
Now, if that applies to England, France and the United States it certainly applies with equal, if not greater, force to Canada. The last country I shall mention is Australia. Paragraph 8, Customs Tariff (Industries Preservation Act) reads:
(1) If the minister is satisfied, after inquiry and report by the Tariff Board, that the exchange value of the currency of the country of origin or export of any goods has depreciated, and that by reason of such depreciation goods have been or are being sold to an importer in Australia at prices which will be detrimental to an Australian industry, the minister may publish a notice in the Gazette specifying the country as to the exchange value of the currency of which he is so satisfied, and the goods originated in or exported from that country to which in his opinion the provisions of this section should apply.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) says that if you want to prohibit Germany from sending goods here you should say so. I am certainly not advocating that. He says::
If you want to say that German goods shall be prohibited say so; if you shrink from saying that in such a direct way, then put on a 1,000 per cent duty.
It is not necessary to do that. Just put a value on German goods for tariff purposes that you would put on similar goods produced in Canada. Take the Canadian selling price of similar goods as the basis on which to value the German goods and put a reasonable duty upon them so as to give the Canadian factories a fair chance to compete with German exports on even terms. Before leaving this point I would refer to a statement made by Mr. Tom Moore, president of the Trades and Labour Congress, after his return from a visit to Germany in 1921. He said:
Skilled mechanics in Germany must work one day to earn the currency which will purchase one pound of butter; they must work one week to earn a pair of shoes, or one month to earn a suit of clothes.
The Minister of Finance, in concluding his very able speech, referred at some length to the subject of capital and labour, declaring that the condition of labour in
this country should not be placed again on a pre-war basis. I am entirely in accord with the remarks of the hon. gentleman in that direction. But if we are going to pass legislation practically preventing the immigration of certain races into this country because we believe that their entry into Canada would have a tendency to lower the standard of living of our own working people, then I hope that the Minister of Finance, who I am sure is sincere in the view he has expressed, that the Canadian labourer should receive a fair and reasonable degree of protection, will give further consideration to the question of the values that are to be put on German goods, and will take such steps as will fairly and adequately protect the workingmen and commerce of this Dominion.
We have been told for a long time now that we have a high protective tariff in Canada, and I have often wondered whether hon. members, particularly my hon. friends on the left, who are of this opinion, have really studied the subject at all, and have given any thought to the tariff conditions under which the United States has come to its present state of prosperity. I am not going to advocate to-day that Canada needs the same high tariff that the United States has had for some considerable time -their tariff has averaged from 1870 to to-day between 47 and 57 per cent on imported articles. I do say, however, that the fact that the United States has seen fit to impose such high tariffs on goods entering that country is a very considerable argument in support of the contention that if we are to have factories in Canada, whether they are ten or twenty years old, such factories, except perhaps lumber, pulp and paper, cannot reasonably be expected to compete with American factories ten times their size, which can easily and with slight added cost manufacture an extra eleventh or twelfth of surplus and ship it here. Our factories cannot stand up against such competitors unless they are afforded a fair protection that will equalize the conditions that exist between the cost of production on an enormous scale, as is the case in the United States, and the cost of production on an average scale, or one-' tenth of the American production, as in the case of Canada.
My hon. friends to my left say that they believe in the development of the basic industries of the country. Now, I suppose that coal would fairly be regarded as a basic commodity, although one hon. gentleman
The Budget-Mr. Bristol

says that there is no such thing as raw material except earth, air and water. However, I conceive that coal, so long as it is in the ground and untouched, is a raw material; and the same is no doubt true of iron. After the United States civil war in 1868, the manufacturers of that country were practically forced to go out of business as a result of the operations of the war. But the Americans saw that they had deposits of iron and coal in close juxtaposition and they made up their minds that they would become the dominating factors in the iron and steel world. At that time England and Germany, particularly England, were supreme in the iron and steel business. The Americans, however, in 1868, put on a general tariff of 37 per cent on imported articles. In 1870 they raised the tariff on articles to 47 per cent, cutting it down 10 per cent in 1872. In 1875 they put it back again at 47 per cent. The Democratic low tariff of 1894 was 37 per cent, and the Dingley tariff of 1897 was an increase to 57 per cent, that tariff practically continuing in force on imported articles until 1909, or almost up to the period of the Great war. After the civil war, in the year 1871, the United States put on a duty of $28 per ton on steel rails. The gross product of the United States in that year was 34,100 tons, and over half a million tons were imported. The average price at that time was $91.70 in the United States and $57.70 in England, the American price exceeding the English price by $34. By 1885 there were produced in the United States 967,000 tons of rails and only 2,200 tons were imported from England. The American price had come down to $28.50, the English price being $23.65, or an excess of the American price over the English price of $4.85. In 1883 the industry had so far progressed that the tariff was reduced from $28 to $17. By 1890 the tariff was further redficed to $13.44. In 1890 the United States produced 1,871,400 tons of steel rails, not one ton being imported, and the difference between the English and the American prices was $4.45 in favour of the United States. In 1897, the duty had been reduced to $6.72, and the quantity of rails produced was 1,630,000 tons, no rails being imported. The average price of the United States produce was $19.60 per ton, the English price being $21, or $1.40 more than that of the United States. To-day steel rails in the United States are on the free list. There is no country in the world today that has iron ore deposits in such vast quantities and of such high grade as has 
the United States in Pennsylvania and Minnesota. When the world war came the United States was supreme in the steel industry, and it has achieved that position under a tariff of the kind I have described which had absolutely excluded English and German rails, with the result that domestic rails were reduced to a lower price in the United States than in any other country in the world.
But let me tell my hon. friends something more; it relates to the German situation. A short time ago certain German companies bought 500,000 tons of Wabana ore in Newfoundland, which they are taking over to Germany and turning into steel rails, and those rails they are able to sell in Cufba in competition with the United States rails. That is what German competition means in rail to-day. Since the war the United States Steel Corporation, which, I suppose, is one of the best organized and most powerful corporations in the world, has not been able to successfully compete against German rails and steel in other parts of the world. That is an added reason for my argument that Canadian workingmen and manufacturers should be protected against German competition.
A similar illustration as to the value and benefit of a protective tariff in building up the iron and steel industry may be taken in the case of nails, on which the duty was originally $80; now they are on the free list. When the duty was first imposed the United States was buying millions of dollars' worth of nails in Eng- . land and Germany; to-day their own manufacturers are able to meet the whole domestic demand.
In the great province of Nova Scotia we find fifteen per cent of the coal deposits of the world. At Wabana, in Newfoundland, is one of the largest ore deposits in the world. Cape Breton and Wabana are in just that position. But what is their relation so far as competitive conditions with the United States are concerned? The deepest United States coal mines to-day are not more than one thousand feet, the shafts are a mile apart, ventilation and haulage are easy, and in many places in Pennsylvania the mines are on the sides of hills or mountains, the coal is brought down an easy slope, and the working conditions enable mining to be carried on at a minimum cost. The result is that in the United States to-

The Budget*-Mr. Bristol
day the miners of bituminous coal produce just twice as much per man as the miners can produce in Nova Scotia, no matter how hard they may work. The cost of coal is largely the cost of mining it. So it is essential that we should build up the coal industry in Nova Scotia, for it would never do for this country to be at the mercy of the United States for soft coal as we are for anthracite coal. But we would be at their mercy if we allowed United States coal to be dumped here at a price that would put our Nova Scotia mines out of business; those mines must be granted reasonable protection. What that reasonable protection should be is a matter for investigation, but there is no doubt of the disparity in conditions, it costing just twice as much to bring a ton of coal to the surface in Nova Scotia as in Pennsylvania. It takes four tons of coal to make a ton of coke for use in the steel industry. If it is costing you twice as much to get your coal, you can figure what your steel is going to cost you. Mining coal in Cape Breton is a submarine proposition, and when you go down two and a quarter miles under the sea, haulage and ventliation are costly and difficult factors, and it takes twice as much time and money to get your ooal out as it would if it comes up a straight shaft, and this additional expense cannot be avoided. Then again the Mesaba iron ore is dug out with a steam shovel; the Wabana ore has to be blasted out under the sea. The adverse conditions in Wabana ore are not so bad as in regard to our Cape Breton coal, but it is infinitely more costly mining ore at Wabana than at Mesaba, in Minnesota, and the latter ore is of higher grade.
It follows from the start that we cannot compete on even terms with the steel industry of the United States either in regard to coal or iron. Now, are we to follow the policy of my hon. friends to my left and say to Nova Scotia: You Shall have no protection; we will tie up your coal mines for two or three hundred years until the American mines are down two thousand or three thousand feet, or they are exhausted-are we to adopt that course? Or are we to follow the policy which has been followed for the last forty years and give reasonable protection and assistance to our Nova Scotia coal and steel industries? It seems to me that if you are to develop your basic industries you must recognize the competitive conditions under which they have to be developed. When I say to you that, as against the protection of $28 to the United States steel rail industry, you can see that our industry is not over-protected, or even sufficiently protected to equalize conditions with American competitors. It also explains why so many steel rails are imported, and why we have our Algoma mills using American coal and iron instead of Canadian or British.
I suppose that if the Minister of Finance had not come from Nova Scotia he might have been a little more just to that province. But I do say as a Canadian who has investigated the matter that I do not think the great province of Nova Scotia has received fair play for her coal and iron industries. Coming into Confederation, she was practically shut out of the American market which she would have had in Boston and New York by water, and was forced to send her products by the long rail haul from Sydney to Montreal before a substantial market is found, except the demand from Nova Scotia railway companies. Moreover, American steel plants at Buffalo are next door to Ontario where a large demand exists for steel products. The fact of the matter is, as one distinguished member on the other side said, the tariff is a compromise. What we have to do is to be fair to each other and to every one. Give every one a square deal, no matter whether he be a farmer, a workingman, or a manufacturer; let us try to treat every one fairly and reasonably. Ontario and Quebec are undoubtedly in favour of a protective tariff; you could not get either of these great provinces to vote againsl such a system. But they would all be in favour of a revision of the tariff; there is not a manufacturer who does not want to see the tariff put on a fair basis. If any manufacturer is getting too much protection the duties in that case should be reduced. Tariff revision is long overdue.
But the tariff should be applied in relation to particular things; this slapping on of a big duty on everything is not the proper method to adopt. Some industries require more protection than others, and the problem is a matter for investigation by a committee so that such protection may be afforded as is proper to develop our natural resources and give our workingmen fair competitive conditions with their fellow-workers in every other country in the world. That is what I stand for.
The Budget-Mr. Bristol

I have every consideration for the farmer of the Canadian West. As far as I can find out he is up against a hard proposition. I know that the purchasing power he ought to have to-day he has not got. I know that if the old dumping clause is retained the British Columbia fruit farmer will be all right; if he gets the protection he wants the Ontario farmer will be all right; the Quebec farmer is always all right; and down in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick they are working hard but they are not getting just as good results as they should for the work they do. But the fact is that Ontario and Quebec get the best bargain at present, British Columbia coming about third. Now, just what can be done to help the condition of the western farmer I am not prepared to say, but undoubtedly it is a matter that should be most carefully investigated by the best brains of the country. But I wish to tell the western farmer, with all the force I can, that I think he is barking up the wrong tree when he says that his only method of securing relief is to change our tariff system. I do not believe that, and I will tell him why in a few words. I agree that he should have relief, but I say, get it some other way. A fair reduction of freight rates would probably give him more purchasing power, and undoubtedly he is entitled to some benefit, because he is not getting any substantial relief out of our protective system. He sells No. 1 Hard wheat, which is the standard for the world, and as he is the only one who raises it his wheat fixes the world price. But I want to say to him that this question of protection is not simply a matter between the farmer of Canada and the manufacturer of Canada, because you have five million farmers to the south of the line, all of whom we must assume to be nearly as wise as Mr. Henry Wise Wood, and they are all opposed to free trade; they want protection, even against the Canadian farmers, I do not blame them for that; their reason is a very simple one. Before the world war the United States was an exporting country, largely of foodstuffs; upon the conclusion of the war they did not want to export foodstuffs because they did not think the fellow on the other side could pay for them. With this market gone, both for manufactured goods and for foodstuffs, the people on-the other side of the line looked askance at Canada when she shipped $175,000,000 worth of foodstuffs into the United States; so they decided to put up the tariff and keep that Canadian stuff out. Of 
course, that did not apply to our No. 1 Hard wheat, for the simple reason that the United States people must have that wheat for seeding purposes and for mixing with other grain to produce a flour of sufficiently good quality to make the bread that the United States people want. So that the matter of the duty does not have so substantial an effect in the case of the No. 1 Hard wheat; the Americans have to buy it, anyway. In the case of cattle, the duty has unquestionably hurt Canadian trade. But why allow so many commodities to come in from the United States-
4 p.m. early strawberries, for instance, and various kinds of early fruits and vegetables? Why not put a high tax on them, and let the Canadian people wait a little while until they can get similar commodities produced in their own country? As a matter of fact, these things are more or less luxuries. In British Columbia they have protection on their fruit. But we in Ontario get all the early potatoes, beans and vegetables of various kinds shipped into Ontario from the United States. Why should we allow that, when the United States does not allow our stuff to go in free? That is what I do not understand. You are level-headed farmers, and I cannot see why the other fellow should be allowed to come into Canada and obtain the benefit of our market when he will not let you get into his.
Now, in this matter of protection, you are the only farmers in the world who are asking for what is involved in your proposed changes in the budget. Look at it from another point of view: what country in the world has been more prosperous since the war than Canada has been? True, you had a bad year last year in your business, but I do not know of anybody who did not have a bad year in business last year. We have good years and we have bad years. Before the war we used to have about only one good year in seven, and then we used to think we were well off. But the war, unfortunately, sent around a good deal of easy money; it got people into expensive habits; and it is a little hard, perhaps, to get away from those habits and settle down to the hard work and the saving which are the only producers of a country's real wealth.
Suppose for one moment that your ideal of free trade were carried out: Take the case of agricultural implements, upon which some reduction has been (made by this budget. The agricultural implement industry in this country is a very important

The Budget-Mr. Bristol
one; thousands of men in Canada-at least, in Ontario and Quebec-are employed in it. Last year the Massey-Harris Company, I happen to know, was working only up to one-sixth of its capacity. During this period our western farmers, for reasons of their own, bought about $11,000,000 worth of American agricultural implements. They paid duty on these implements, and felt that Canada was getting the benefit of that duty. But if you had paid out this $11,000,000 in Canada, the Massey-Harris Company and all the other implement manufacturing firms in Quebec and Ontario would have been enabled to work full time and you would not have had men to feed who were unemployed; there would have been no starving families and no unemployment in this part of the world. It is true you paid the customs duties, but what else did you do? You patriotic men sent your money away to pay the working men of the United States, t<j assist in the building up of American industries, to feed American mouths, when there were Canadian mouths in want of food. If only from the point of view of common, decent charity to your fellow-countrymen who fought ibeside you during the war, you should have bought these thing in Canada, even if it cost a little more to do so. It is only by the rounded-out prosperity of the country generally that you get increased population, that you get growth and development, that you get a market and create ability to buy the things which you produce.
But, you may say, that is a selfish way to look at it. I do not know exactly what effect the 2i per cent reduction which has been made will bring about, but I doubt if it will make a difference of $10 a year to any one of you gentlemen who are farmers. But it will make a lot of difference if. it shuts down the agricultural implement factories of this country. If you have this free trade that you want, you think that you are going to get things cheaper. Well, you would get them cheaper, if the world would just stand still and these things would simply come into Canada as before and nothing more would happen. But you know as well as I do-probably a good deal better-that if the agricultural inmplement factories of this country are shut down and can no longer compete with the American agricultural implement factories; if the Harvester Company goes back to Chicago, where it belongs; if the 350 American factories, which have spent over $100,000,-
000	in the last thirty years in the building of big factories in this country, shut down in Canada and return to the United States, -which would mean a saving in overhead -you know that they will be able to sell these implements to you at such prices as they may demand. We have no control , over American factories, American trusts, American prices. You really do not believe, do you, that the Harvester Company, with no competition in Canada, would sell you your mowers and binders more cheaply? If you do, look at the history of Australia. Australia had a labour party; they wanted free trade and they got it, but they have now gone in for high protection-60 jper cent on agricultural! implements. You know that, and you know the result has been that the Massey-Harris Company and others have had to go into Australia, establish works there, and give employment to Australian workingmen. Well, if we had free trade the same would happen here-you would be eaten alive; almost before the legislation was passed, the American trusts-would control the Canadian market and would charge you fifty per cent more than any Canadian company had ever charged you. You do not think the United States trusts are benevolent institutions existing for the benefit of western Canada, do you? I assure you they are not. Why, we could not do anything. The trusts and combines in this country, about which your leader was talking a great deal during the campaign

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. The hon. member is too old and too experienced a parliamentarian to forget that he must address the Chair.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Marquette (Mr. Crerar), during the recent campaign, was speaking on the question of trusts and combines; I think the question of the -woollen industry was one that bothered him, as it did another hon. gentleman last night. He was telling us of the terrible duty of 35 per cent on woollens.
1	looked the matter up and I found that about $60,000,000 worth of woollen goods were imported into this country last year, but they were imported from England, not from the United States, and the British preference, which is, I think, about 50 per cent, perhaps less, made the duty only 17i per cent-which was the tariff rates as in force at the time of the Mackenzie government.
The Budget-Mr. Bristol

But to come back to the argument I am trying to present, I wish to point out that if you have free trade you put yourself at the mercy of the factories of Germany, of England and of the United States, because you put your own Canadian factories out of business by unfair competition. It is obvious that there is practically nothing outside of pulpwood timber and that sort of thing, that we could manufacture in competition with the United States. If, then, you do that, it must be obvious to you that although you are getting the highest price for wheat, you are dealing a body blow to the industries of Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and, possibly, Manitoba. And what else have you done? You h'ave put the farmers in these great provinces out of business, because if the factories are not running in Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton and the other large cities of this country, the farmer has no home market, -and on the question of home market, I would mention the county of York concerning which the leader of the Government knows something so far as the home market is concerned. But that is the position: if you have free trade you have ruined the eastern farmers and manufacturers. As I have said, you still get the highest price for your No. 1 hard wheat, which is the best wheat in the world. Then what becomes of the rest of us? We shall not oe here and you will have the national debt on your hands. I do not suppose you would agree with the member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) in the suggestion that the debt ought to be repudiated. You certainly would not be able to adopt his alternative suggestion and have a capital levy under those conditions.

speechtext:
Will the hon. member
permit a question?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: With pleasure.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

If the wheat growers
should leave the prairie provinces, apparently all the rest of Canada would automatically disappear?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Not at all. Why do
you say that?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Did you not say that the
manufacturer would be ruined, as well as the Ontario farmer, if we brought our goods in free?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You would still be raising your No. 1 hard wheat, the best there is, and selling it in the markets of the 
world at he highest price. I said the rest of us would be out of business and that Canada would be at he mercy of the trusts in the United States who instead of producing twelve times as much as they do to-day, would manufacture for Canada an additional thirteen times if the Canadians are forced to use their products and Canadian factories are out of business, and at their own prices. That is practically what it would amount to. View the matter in any way you like there is no escape from that conclusion.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If there is no escape from that conclusion as my hon. friend says, if we are forced to leave the prairie provinces and quit producing where are you going to deliver the goods that you manufacture?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why, we are not shipping to you to that extent, are we?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, but you say that if we do not buy your goods you will not be able to keep your factories going.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, I am not saying
that at all. I simply say that if your free trade doctrines were to go into effect you will ruin the eastern manufacturers, with the exception, of course, the manufacturers of pulp, paper and lumber, and you will ruin substantially the eastern farmer. On the face of it, you in the West will be just as prosperous, the only difference being that you will have to pay for your manufactured products any price that the United States trusts choose to ask for them, and you will have the national debt of this country on your hands-that is alL And you are getting perilously near that condition now in connection with the manufacture of agricultural implements in this country. Because, before the war the agricultural implement manufacturers in Canada, particularly the Massey-Harris company, had a tremendous and growing trade in Europe, especially in Germany and Russia. That market is gone to-day, with a loss of many millions of dollars. We do not know whether they can weather present conditions or not; if they do not, you will have to pay more for your agricultural implements.
The point I was trying to make, as far as I was able to do so, is that every civilized country in the world-except the community represented by the farmers of western Canada-are in favour of the protective principle, in favour of protecting their home industries. I have also tried

The Budget-Mr. Bristol
to point out that the suggested change in the method of raising the revenue would not be in the interest of the western farmers any more than it would he in the interest of their fellow countrymen. I do not question the sincerity of the motives which actuate my hon. friends from the West. I believe they are influenced by sincere and patriotic motives; and it is only by all of us discussing our respective viewpoints that we can get results. I sincerely trust that in Canada we will all try to work together, eastern men with western men. I certainly recognize that agriculture is the basic industry of Canada, and that no country can be great and prosperous unless its agriculture is prosperous, and its workingmen are sufficiently paid, happy and contented. I want to see the best of feeling existing between the great provinces of Ontario and Quebec

and let me say here I was very glad that one of my hon. friends from Montreal went up to Toronto the other day and delivered a speech to our friends up there along this line. Let us continue our efforts to secure unity, because there should be no differences between us. There should be harmony not only between these two provinces, but between eastern and western Canada. Because we are all patriotically endeavouring, in our own way, to work for our common country and to obtain the best possible results.
There are many features in connection with the existing situation that require consideration, but one difficulty at present is this. Deflation is required in two items which affect almost everybody; one is rent and the cost of building,- and the other is the cost of coal to heat our homes. Now, I have never been able to understand why the building trades and building unions of this country-composed of reasonable and intelligent men as they are-have not been willing to accept reasonable prices for building material and reasonable rates of wages; why they have not been willing to cut down in the matter of prices and wages as the farmer has had to cut down the price of his products. If that were to take place there would be a tremendous building boom in this country and it would be of enormous benefit to Canada, and our working people in large cities like Toronto and Hamilton would not have to live in boxes lined with paper as many of them do-literally packing boxes. They would have decent houses in which to live and to bring up their families. When I find, for example, the price of brick in a great
city like Montreal is practically $23 a thousand when in my opinion it ought to be about $10, you can readily see what a great handicap there is to building operations. I have no complaint to make against our labour unions. I think our Canadian working men are as fine a lot of men as there are in the world; I do not know that any better are to be found anywhere. But if they would only get together and agree upon reasonable terms there would be millions of money spent upon building, and a greater number of houses would be available at cheap rents. Another necessity is a reasonable price for our coal. There must be deflation in both the directions I have indicated. A labouring man is no better off with $10 per day than with $5 if the latter figure will purchase as much as the former, except that he can say that he has more money in his pocket. The great object should be to get the men engaged in the building trades together and try to arrive at a reasonable rate for the construction of houses so that rents might be cut down and people housed at a moderate figure. Once you can cut into the wages of the men who run the great railways of this country, once you can properly and fairly do that, you can unquestionably effect a great reduction in railway rates; and you certainly have got to have a reduction of railway rates in some way. As between the east and the west, if the east, which benefits more from protection than the west, has to pay a little more in consequence it would perhaps only be fair.
With reference to the amendment, it seems to me purely a question of whether our western friends and the rest of the House want to go on record as saying that no matter what platform you may stand on during the election you can discard that platform when the election is over. If I have any comment to make on the subject it is just this-does the House think it wise for public men to put themselves into such a position that it can be said that no reliance can be placed on their promises? I do not believe that to be in the interest either of this parliament or of the country.
Mr. ANDREW R. McMASTER (Brome): Before entering upon the few observations that I have prepared for this afternoon, may I respond briefly to some of the assertions and arguments advanced so pleasantly by the hon. member who has just taken his seat. First of all, he complains that the
The Budget-Mr. McMaster

Finance Minister should have raised the tariff; if only the tariff is raised everything will be happy in Canada. Now a tariff is a tax, and therefore the logical conclusion is that if we will only tax ourselves a little more heavily all will be well. My hon. friend states that we should be very much afraid of German competition because in Germany the men are working on scales of wages which he read out. Now, there are two possible conclusions from the figures which he gave us. One conclusion is that someone has been telling him fairy tales; the second conclusion is that the purchasing power of the mark in Germany must be very much higher than its international or exchange value, because according to the figures which he gave us the amounts paid to people in Germany would not keep body and soul together; and I think we will all agree that workmen always have to have enough to keep body and soul together or they are not able to work. He states that the German workmen are working ten hours a day if not twelve. That is not in accordance with the information which I have gathered. I have a paper published in New York called the Dry Goods Economist. It is in its 76th year of publication, and has been handed me by a gentleman in whom I have the utmost confidence. I will read an extract from the issue of the 20th May of this year. It says:
Last week, during the convention of the Ninth National Foreign Trade Convention, a speaker who had just returned from Europe quoted Dr. Walter Eathenau, the prominent German publicist, as having declared that Germany is now exporting only 25 per cent of its prewar volume. And that German production costs have been rising rapidly is the statement made to our Commerce Department by its Commercial Attache at Berlin, with the upward tendency still apparent.
We may doubt the statement of Dr. Walter Rathenau because he is a German, but it would be impossible, I think, to doubt the correctness of the information gathered by the American representative in Berlin that production costs in that country are rapidly rising. The article goes on to say however:
Indications, moreover, continue to multiply that Germany has not a great amount of goods to export. A writer in a Berlin trade paper, dated April 23, states that in the first half of the year 1921, as a result of strikes in Germany. 772,891 persons were out of work and that the German industries during that period sustained a loss of 11,608,129 working days.
After all, human nature is somewhat the same all over the world. Workmen

are being asked in all countries of the world to accept harder working conditions and to accept lower pay, and they accept it reluctantly and only after a struggle. I think that what is contained in this article is very much more likely to be true than the information just given to the House by the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Bristol) although I do not infer for a moment that the hon. member would desire to mislead the House. Might I say with all kindness, that his address would appear to be labelled, if the Marking Act were in force " Made in Toronto ". The United States high tariff has been the cause of the prosperity of the United States according to the view of the hon. member, but we know differently. We know the economic history of the United States only shows that a people with boundless natural resources and a virile hardworking and intelligent population can succeed in spite of a very unsound tariff or fiscal policy. The fact of the matter is that, although there has been an ebb of reaction in United States in trade matters, the best commercial, the best industrial and the best financial minds in the United States are more and more tending towards a free trade solution of the difficulties of the world. There was an effort made in the Fordney Bill to put upon the tariff schedules boots and shoes and leather, which are now free, but a great movement came to have them remain on the free list. And from whom? From the shoe manufacturers of United States. " Because " they said, if you put them on a protective tariff schedule, then, of course, those who produce leather, which is our raw material, will demand that leather be put on a tariff schedule and we produce a great deal of boots and shoes for foreign export. We have got to meet the competition of the world. In order to meet the competition of the world we have to have our raw material free, and therefore we believe we will find when the dust of the conflict clears off at Washington concerning the Fordney Bill we will find boots and shoes and leather still on the free list.
Now passing from the United States my hon. friend went back to Germany and said that the Germans had come and bought from Newfoundland some Wabana ore. I mention that in passing merely to illustrate the argument which I propose to make in reply to the argument which he made

The Budget-Mr. McMaster
that the coal mines of Nova Scotia are absolutely unable to endure competition from the United States and that the steel interests of Nova Scotia are absolutely unable to meet the competition of the American steel interests. His argument is this: We have to go under the sea in wet mines for our coal, and in Newfoundland they have to go under the sea in wet mines for our iron ore. But if the iron ore was hard to get out why do the Germans buy it? Why did they not go to the United States where the ore according to his statement was raised with a steam shovel and therefore should be much cheaper? What is the matter with the steel interests or the coal interests of Nova Scotia? They are both combined. Is it the water in the mine or the water in the stock that is the trouble? I know something about the formation of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company. I was only a youth, but I heard the mattei discussed in Montreal, and I know that the great promotor of that industry, H. M Whitney, told investors in Montreal before he invited them to put in any money, in the early days of the concern, that such was the advantage that Nova Scotia possessed with reference to this coal and to the close proximity of iron ore in Nova Scotia, that they could meet the competition of the world. I was wondering whether if that company had not suffered from the watering of stock, the re-watering of stock and the re-re-watering of stock that has taken place, and if it had remained in the hands of the capable honest and high-principled business man that some time ago had control of the company, whether it would be in the condition in which it is to-day. And what is the situation, and what is the conclusion which should be reached?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do I understand the hon. member to state that it would have been better for the company if there had been no Whitnej legislation?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, I made no such assertion. What I did say was this: Mr. Whitney told the interests of Montreal, when the company was formed, that they could stand competition from the world, and I know that when the company was floated the common stock was sold for fifteen cents on the dollar.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Does the hon. member dispute my statement that it costs twice as much to-day to raise a ton of coal to the surface in Cape Breton as it does in Pennsylvania? That was my statement. I did not
go into the watering business or anything else.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am not in a position to contradict the figures given by my hon. friend, that it costs twice as much in Nova Scotia to raise a ton of coal as it does in certain parts of United States; but if he tells me that my statement as to the watering of the stock of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company and the other companies, almost too numerous to remember, which preceded or have succeeded that company is untrue, I would ask him to look at the quotations on the stock exchange of the preferred stock, and the second preferred stock, and the common stock, of that company, and answer me whether, if dollar for dollar had ever gone into that concern, it is likely those stocks would have been quoted at the price at which they are quoted now.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I can only tell my hon.
friend that, with reference to the second preferred stock of the Steel company exchanged for the Dominion common stock, I am aware that the price of $70 a share was paid for 50,000 shares a short time before. I have myself paid $140,000 or more for 2,000 shares, and that money went into the treasury of the company. I do not know about previous transactions, but I know the English syndicate-and they have been very much misrepresented; I know my hon. friend wishes to be fair- men like Lord Furness and others who came in, paid $70 a share for the common stock which is to-day selling at $30.
Mr.-McMASTER: I suppose the shares of the second preferred stock were $100 par. If they were bought at $70, there is 30 per cent of water, at any rate. I do not know whether I made any statement as to the exact amount of water, but I think the company has been very well sprinkled. What is the logical conclusion of what my learned and hon. friend has told us, if we take his statements as being absolutely correct? It is this, that there is no hope in Canada for getting steel rails at prices which would compare with world prices. Nevertheless, we have an annual deficit running from $50,000,000 to $100,000,000 on our National railways. Everything that makes railway construction, whether it be of bridges, or steel rails, or steel cars, or steel wheels, more expensive, is going to increase the deficit on our National railways, which deficit has to come out of our pockets.



The Budget-Mr. McMaster
My learned and hon. friend then turned to Australia, and he said that Australia had had free trade. I do not think, in the recollection of the present generation, Australia was a free trade country. Prior to the confederation of the Australian states, there were two states in Australia, one being a free trade state and the other a protectionist state. A very interesting argument for the benefit of free trade as opposed to protection for industries can be drawn from the fact that the manufacturers of the free trade state in Australia were more prosperous than those in the protectionist state alongside of it.
I do not think the West ever had such a high compliment paid to it as was paid by the hon. member for Centre Toronto. If the people who live in the prairie provinces cease buying goods from eastern Canada, then, he says, we may as well shut up shop. That is a pretty good reason, if true, why we should endeavour to have living conditions such as to encourage people to stay in the western provinces and to encourage more to go there. I think the agricultural implement business is one which could have a very happy and useful life even under the free breath of absolute free trade. As Mr. Findlay, the late manager of the Massey-Harris Company said, "Give the manufacturers of agricultural implements our raw materials free and we will meet the world." That is the evidence given by Mr. Findlay, the manager, himself. I have endeavoured, very inadequately, I am sure, to deal with what has been stated by the hon. member (Mr. Bristol) who has just taken his seat.
The task of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) is one of the heaviest that has ever been before a Minister of Finance of this country. When he was appointed, when the ministry was formed, the Minister of Finance said: "Cabinet ministers are subjects for sympathy rather than for congratulation." I congratulate the Minister of Finance, because he had such a real appreciation of the difficulty of his task; but I know all in this House, irrespective of whatever their view of public policy, whatever their party allegiance, wish the Minister of Finance every help and strength in meeting the situation which confronts him. May I tender him my warmest congratulations on courageously doing away with those underhand methods of giving protection to special interests in this country which were found in the Depreciation of Currency Act, the Marking Act, the Certification Act and some other acts, the names

of which I have forgotten for the moment? I believe he is entitled to the highest commendation for his action in that regard. We have had some criticism of his attitude from members of the official Opposition. Some of this criticism has been couched in kindly and polite language, such as was use! by the hon. member who has just spoken. Other criticism has been uttered in language which I do not hesitate to characterize as grossly unfair. The hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton), who formerly occupied the high position of Minister of Finance of this country, stated that this was a budget giving a preference to Great Britain and free trade to Germany. I think the hon. gentleman rather fell below his usual level when he made that statement, and it was unworthy of one who held high office in this country. For anyone to try to introduce international bitterness and hate into the discussion of a business matter is, I believe, highly undesirable. Moreover, the statement is not true. The tariff remains on German goods at the general tariff rate, which is, in many cases, a high rate. The argument used by the ex-Minister of Finance was an interesting one. He seemed to think that the prosperity of a country was helped by two things-perhaps I should say that he seemed to think that the prosperity of a country, as regards the possibility and power of exporting goods and entering into competition with the world, was helped by two things; first by a depreciated currency, and second by a low standard of living. How can we expect, says he, the Canadian workmen to comnete with the workman who is earning only a few dollars a week? I doubt if there is any advantage in a depreciated currency as regards payment of wages in a country because depreciated currency means merely an inflated currency, and as a rule, when you inflate currency, you inflate prices at the same time, in just about the same proportion. I do not, therefore, see how there can be any real advantage in that regard ; but I am perfectly certain that, when a country with an inflated or a depreciated currency goes outside to purchase, any possibility of advantage disappears; and Germany, which after all is a country of northern Europe with a temperate climate, a country having to buy a vast deal of its raw materials outside of the country, when it goes outside, has to pay, not in its depreciated currency-for after all, wealth does not consist in pieces of paper turned out by a printing press, but in real money ac-

The Budget-Mr. McMaster
cording to the standards of the country in which it makes its purchase. I have in my hand a table which has been prepared for me by our Dominion Bureau of Statistics-and we are fortunate, indeed, in having available to members of this House who care to study matters carefully and thoroughly, the assistance of the able and courteous official whom we have at the head of this department, with his no less able and courteous assistants. I have before me the monthly averages of imports for consumption into Germany and exports from Germany. This shows that, in 1913, the monthly average of imports for domestic consumption was almost 900,000,000 marks. Their exports of domestic products totalled almost 842,000,000 marks in 1913. In January of this year they imported over 12,500,000,000 marks' worth of goods and exported in the same month goods to the extent of ever 14,500,000,000 marks. A great deal pf these purchases are purchases in foreign countries of raw materials worked up in Germany and then sent out of that country; and if there be any advantage in depreciated currency so far as paying the home labourer is concerned, it disappears entirely when you come to deal with purchases abroad. I may say that these figures are obtained from the monthly bulletin of statistics of the League of Nations for March, 1922.
Then there is another argument which is very unsound, and which I think is a very dangerous one from the point of view of labour, and that is that cheap labour is inexpensive labour. Cheap labour is very often the most expensive sort of labour. Let me give two examples. When the Panama canal was being built the white labourers were paid in gold and the black labourers in silver. They were paid so many dollars a day, one in gold and the other in silver, and it made a substantial difference between them. But the amount of labour which the white man did over and above that of the black man made the two labour costs practically the same. Again, some time before the war, a commission of investigation on labour costs visited the United States from Great Britain. They found that in many lines of work, wages in the United States were considerably higher than in Great Britain, but that the labour costs were not higher, in many cases being lower. Why? The highly paid, ambitious man getting a good wage and living in a good house is anxious to see his children well educated, and he
therefore puts into his work a force and efficiency which the lower paid man does not. I trust, therefore, that we have disposed of this suggestion that we should change our legislation because of fears from German competition.
Then we have the remarks of the hon. member for St. John and Albert (Mr. Baxter), who thought that the Almighty had not dealt hardly enough with the German people, and who wished to see some German cities devastated. Well, I would remind the hon. gentleman that vengeance belongs to a Higher Power. Hatred forms the seedbed of future wars, and anyone who speaks or writes with the idea of perpetuating national hatred just waters that seedbed and brings forth the seeds to quicker and surer germination. The official Opposition often claim, or speak in such a fashion as to make one believe, that they regard themselves as the official depositories of loyalty to the Empire, as they call it, and of pride in British connection and admiration for British traditions. So far as admiration for British traditions is concerned, I do not give ground to them for one instant. But I say that any desire or attempt to foment and maintain international hatred and bitterness after the fighting is over is not the British way. Let me give two or three examples to illustrate this truth. Quebec was taken in 1759 at the close of the Seven Years' War. Now, I am sure that there had been many atrocities committed on both sides in that war, because both races on the North American Continent had the aid of their savage allies, the Indians. While the siege of Quebec was in progress the farms and farmhouses of the French-Canadian habitants in that neighbourhood were devastated. The French-Canadian looked forward with fear and trembling to what would happen after the capitulation. But what did happen? The day after the capitulation, Amherst said to his soldiers: " These French-Canadians are now your fellow-citizens; treat them as such." Three weeks afterwards, speaking in their own tongue to the French-Canadians, he said: You are now British subjects, entitled to the rights of such. I have told my soldiers to treat you as fellow citizens; see that you treat them in the same way. What ensued? A few weeks after, the Tommy Atkins of that day was. helping the habitant bring in his crops; and it was not more than a month or two
