speechtext:
A protectionist convinced against his will is of his own opinion still. Now, I have the figures for 1907 for Holland. In 1907 Holland, I see, laid a tax of B per cent on manufactured goods. I assume that in this case I can answer my right hon. friend, (Mr. Meighen) who is modestly sitting in the rear; those goods, I imagine, must come into competition with other goods made in Holland. On raw material and necessaries of life it was 2 per cent and 3 per cent, and as the total taxation in 1912 was less than one-half of one per cent, I presume that foodstuffs must have come in free. Holland, I should think, is in exactly the same position as Denmark; they are splendid agricultural countries; their agriculture is developed to a very high point of perfection, and they will have no protection upon food.
I think I might now pass to what I would call the great example of free trade, and that is the country which, I believe, has the honour of having been the native place of the member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond)-Great Britain. Let me deal first with the Key Industries Act. If there ever was a case, Mr. Speaker, of_ much cry and little wool, it has been the joy of the protectionists over the Key Industries Act. The Key Industries Act affords a protection, it is true, 331 per cent on the articles included in a certain schedule, but if that schedule came into contact with the schedules in a real protectionist country, it would be absolutely lost; it is so small you would not be able to find it. It could be printed on half a page of this book which I hold in my hand. It deals with the most restricted classes of goods:	optical glass
and optical elements; theodolites, beakers, flasks, burettes, measuring cylinders, thermometers, tubing, and other scientific glassware, and lamp-blown ware; galvanometers, pyrometers, electroscopes, barometers, wireless valves and similar rectifiers-I will not read the whole list. The point I want to make is that the amount of goods which come under the Safeguarding of Industries Act is infinitesimal compared with the amount which goes free into the Old Land. Then there is provision for the imposition of a duty should a committee decide that certain goods are being sold in too keen competition with British goods. But the interests of the consumer are well safeguarded under the Key Industries Act. First of all there is provided a committee which must sit and investigate the case, and appeal may be had by any interest affected

to a court of appeal constituted by the Lord Chancellor of England. This board may make an order, but if Parliament is going to sit within one month, that order cannot go into effect. If our protectionist friends would be willing to put their whole claim for protection under this act I do not know whether even such a convinced free trader as myself would not at least take it into earnest and sympathetic consideration.
What is the history of the free trade movement in England? Was it that English industry was built up under protection? -industry which takes the raw material from the fellaheen, the negro and the other persons who work in the hot parts of the earth to produce cotton and jute and cocoa and rubber and all those things which are used in the industries of Great Britain. Was it under protection? No, it was not. In 1721, first of all, Walpole started to take off duties. Then from 1823 to 1826, Huskisson took off a great number of duties. Then there was the great free trade agitation from 1837 to 1846, when John Bright and Richard Cobden, those two great apostles not only of free trade but of international brotherhood and of reason between man and man and between nation and nation, went throughout the length and breadth of the land. We had the repeal of the corn laws, and in 1860 we had the final doing away with duties. And what happened? Their trade went forward by leaps and bounds; their shipping increased by the hundreds and the thousands and the tens of thousands of tons. I cannot take the time of the House to go into the matter in detail but let me say that by reason of that free trade policy Great Britain not only became, for long, long years, the premier manufacturing country of the world, but she became the carrier, she became the banker, she became the insurer, for a great part of the whole known world. Prior to 1850-prior, indeed, to 1860-the United States, the other great nation of the world, carried fifty per cent of her own imports and her own exports in her own bottoms. The Stars and Stripes floated in nearly every sea; in nearly every port you could see the clipper-built ships of the United States-aye, and the clipper-built ships of Nova Scotia, because, although the United States stood on a high eminence at that time in the matter of shipping, alongside them were the sailors from the little province of Nova Scotia. But what happened after 1860? As the gentleman from Centre Toronto (Mr. Bristol) has said, protection was put on in the United States.

The Budget-Mr. McMaster
And protection "protected" the merchant marine of the United States almost out of existence, so that in 1900 not ten per cent of American imports and exports were carried in their own bottoms. There were other contributing factors, of course, but that is one; and I think the House and those of us who believe in the doctrines of free trade are deeply indebted to the member for Brantford for having brought before us this splendid example of how free trade helps nations to develop their secondary industries.
Now, I wish to deal for a short time with the budget itself. Let me say that I make the suggestions which I
5 p.m. have to make in a spirit of sincere diffidence and modesty. I am making suggestions to a finance minister who was my leader-and who is my leader-in matters of finance for very many years. I suppose the first time I heard the Minister of Finance speak was when I was a student in Montreal, on the occasion of a by-election, when we elected Jimmy McShane over Dr. William Kingston. The minister spoke in the old Windsor Hall-and ah, what a night was that! There was the Minister of Finance; there was Sir Wilfrid Laurier; there was the late Mr. Emmerson, from New Brunswick; and last but not least there was the Guys-borough giant, D. C. Fraser, of Antigonish. The principles which were set forth then were the principles which were to guide the Liberal party. I believed in those principles then; I believe in those principles now, and in the light of those principles I propose to examine the budget.
The sales tax provisions are not what the member for Southeast Grey (Miss Mac-phail) described them to be-a step backward. I think the hon. member described the taking off of the 21 per cent as a step forward and the putting on of the sales tax as a step backward. Well, that is not quite fair, because a sales tax goes not only upon the goods brought into the country but also upon goods manufactured in the country, and a great deal more of the resulting proceeds go into the coffers of the state. Now, I am stupid about figures; I like if possible to get things down in concrete shape, because I feel, Mr. Speaker, that if I myself understand them other people should be able to understand them as well. So I put this in a concrete way; I think I have arrived at the right facts, and I trust that my conclusions will commend themselves to the House. If a bolt of cloth be manufactured in Canada and sold by the
manufacturer to the jobber, the manufacturer will add to his invoice 21 per cent under the new regulations. This amount the jobber will pay to the manufacturer who will account for it to the Government. That is the first step. Now the jobber when he comes to re-sell to the retailer has to add to his price the 21 per cent he paid to the manufacturer, and then, of course, if he is doing business on proper lines he must add to that his ordinary profit. Now let us suppose that the jobber is satisfied with an ordinary profit of 10 per cent-sometimes he will get more, sometimes he will get less; but I suppose 10 per cent is not an unfair profit to estimate. Therefore the tax when the goods arrive at the retailers amounts to 21 per cent imposed by the manufacturer, plus 21 per cent. That makes 41 per cent plus profit -say 10 per cent to the jobber on the 21 per cent he has had to advance to the manufacturer, which is between one-fifth and one-fourth of a cent. Hence the retailer finds his purchase increased not by 41 but by 41 per cent. On this he bases his profit. Now what a retailer's profit is it is sometimes difficult to say. I have heard of one large house which puts a hundred per cent on. I think that is profiteering, and as I like to quote people who, I believe, are doing the right thing, we will call it 40 per cent. That will include 40 per cent of the 41 per cent; so when it finally arrives to the consumer who pays it he does not pay 41 per cent but a higher amount-the consumer pays 61 per cent, that is to say if ordinary business methods are followed. Of course sometimes a jobber will absorb it, sometimes the merchant will absorb it; but I think as a general rule that under ordinary canons of business that tax of 41 per cent will be 61 per cent before it reaches the consumer. Now, if the bolt of cloth is manufactured in Canada and sold directly to the retailer by the mill-and that often happens-then the tax is 41 per cent, there is only one profit to add, so that the ultimate consumer will bear 61 per cent instead of, as it is, 61 per cent. But suppose the bolt of cloth is manufactured in Bradford. It is sold to a jobber in Ottawa, re-sold by him to a retailer in Almonte, and sold by him to a minister of the gospel who is a member of the House of Commons on the Progressive side.

We are not allowed
here to name people by name. Now how does that work out? The duty under the new schedule, the duty on this bolt of

The Budget-Mr. McMaster
cloth, is 271 per cent, and the sales tax is 4i per cent, which makes the aggregate impost when the cloth comes into this country 32 per cent. When that cloth reaches the consumer the jobber will have to have his profit on the duty which is advanced to the Government, if he imported it, and it will also have to bear the profit of the retailer. So I calculate that if we give the jobber his 10 per cent, and give the retailer his 40 per cent, we will make the duty borne by the consumer of this bolt of cloth 49 per cent and of this impost the sales tax and the profits on the sales tax amount to 5i per cent. Now if the bolt of cloth is sold directly by the manufacturer in Bradford to the retailer in Almonte, the sales tax is 6 per cent and the duty will be 331 per cent; and if the cloth was manufactured in Lowell, Massachusetts, the duty would be 41 per cent, and the duty borne by the consumer would be 41 per cent plus 40 per cent or 571 per cent. Now what are the deductions that I make? First of all it seems to me that the imposing of a heavier duty, on the sale of the goods manufactured at home from the manufacturer or producer to the retailer

a heavier rate of duty than is borne in the case where the manufacturer sells to the jobber and the jobber then sells to the retailer-really discourages the elimination of the middleman. I know that an apparent unfairness, perhaps a real unfairness, might take place if we did not so increase the rate of the sales tax in that case; hut I do say that one of the undesirable features of this sales tax is that it encourages the maintenance of the middleman or discourages his elimination. Now that is one, and I do not think a very important, direct objection to the tax, but where I think-and I submit this with a good deal of confidence-the tax is undesirable is the imposition of the sales tax on goods which, on entering this country, already pay a high customs duty. Because what happens? This may very possibly, may very likely, happen: That it makes very little difference whether you call it an impost, or a sales tax, or a protective or revenue duty-if the impost amounts to a high percentage the goods may not come in at all, and the revenue by that fact suffers. That is a point that should be borne in mind; and I respectfully ask the Finance Minister to carefully consider as to whether it would not be better to make these sales taxes, in reality what they are in name, excise taxes-to have them to a certain extent as counter-[ Mr. McMaster. ]
vailing duties. In that way we will get more money for the state and we will, in my humble opinion, substantially relieve the consumer.
Now I have dealt with the advantages of the sales tax over the mere imposition of customs duty by the tariff. The cuts are smaller than I had hoped for-smaller indeed than I believe I had reason to expect. If the Finance Minister will pardon me I cannot very well say that it is the quick, decisive step that he customarily takes in the right direction; I would say it is a short shuffle generally in the right direction. I am doubtful, too, about the advisability of waiting to see how the Americans are going to deal with their tariff before dealing with our own, but I say this: I am not going to take issue with the Finance Minister in that regard because he may have information which he is unable, naturally, to convey to the House, information which he has learned on his recent trip to Washington and which leads him to think that it is good tactics not to declare our cuts immediately. But I would remind him respectfully of what Peel said in 1841, that "the way to overcome hostile tariffs was by free imports."
Why do I accept this budget, with less enthusiasm however than I would like to have accepted it? Why do I accept it? I accept it, reserving my right to criticise any items of importance when we are in committee on the resolutions. I do so because I am unprepared to believe that the Liberal party has been, or will be, recreant to its history on the trade question. I sometimes think that some of my friends opposite are not quite as fair as they should be to the Liberal party in regard to what they did in connection with the tariff. We came in in 1896, and we did make substantial reductions in the customs duty. Open confession is good for the soul. I never pretended to be pleased with the revision of the tariff of 1904. We had increased the British preference until it was a full 331 per cent, but in 1904, in response to that pressure which is constantly brought upon the government by organized protected interests of this country, which is not offset by the consuming interests as they should offset it,-in response to that pressure there were certain increases in lines of textiles, woollen cloth, tweed and wearing apparel and on twine and cordage, and slight reductions were made on china and window glass. Then we had the revision of 1907. As to that revision I am not prepared to say whether that was a

The Budget-Mr. McMaster
revision which on the whole reduced or increased the British preference. I have in my hand a statement of the textile items of the tariff, and I find there were decreases in 18 items, and there were increases in 18 items, and no change in 9 items, and no change in 14 items on the free list. There were 59 textile items in the customs tariff of 1907 and they were divided, as I say. Whether the increases were greater than the decreases I do not know, but I am sorry the decreases in the preference were made, and 1 am glad the increases in the preference were made. But whatever our backslidings in the past were, what we did in 1911 should be accounted to us for righteousness. I suppose I will get the name in this House of being a candid friend, disagreeing at times with everybody but not necessarily all at the same time, but I do not think the Liberal party has had quite as much credit from the western friends as it should have for what we did in 1911. In 1878 the Liberal party went down to defeat because it stood up for the rights of the consuming public against the organized protected manufacturers of this country. In 1911 they did the same thing, and they met the same fate. AVe were not altogether blameless in the matter, and I will tell the House why. Because, from 1904 to 1911 we had, doubtless because of perfectly natural and reasonable causes, a pressure of work on ministers which was abominable and abnormal- more than it should be, we had not been preaching our gospel as we should have preached it, and generation after generation of young men came to the age of 21 who had never heard the trade question discussed, who did not know that trade was a good thing in itself and were therefore able to be led astray and beguiled by the specious argument of "no truck or trade with the Yankees", or the statement that our loyalty would be affected if we dealt in potatoes, or apples, or wheat, or barley, or flax, with the United States. But we went down fighting for a great cause. And it is because we have done these things in the past that I propose to maintain my support of the budget in the present instance. We have also the declarations of the Liberal party in connection with the trade policy. We have the Ottawa platform of 1893, and I may say if one will read over this platform of 1893 he will find that everything in it is true, that after having experienced protection from 1878 to 1893 the Liberal party came to the conclusion expressed in their platform was
right, and I say that in the mind of every informed, unprejudiced and disinterested man, everything that happened since that time bears out the truth and soundness of the position we took. I rely upon the statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) in introducing his budget of 1897- which was the beginning of a fresh era for Canada. Now let us be fair to the Liberal party and let us be fair to the Minister of Finance. Canada after 1896 was a different place from what it was prior to that time. The Minister of Finance, who is the Minister of Finance to-day, after having read the Ottawa platform said:
Mr. Speaker, the electors of Canada, in due course, gave their verdict upon that and upon other issues, and subject to such changes as changing circumstances may require, and as to which I shall have something to say as I proceed, we accept the Liberal platform of Ottawa as the declaration of principles which we are bound to follow in our tariff reform.
I pass on to a declaration made by one whose name is ever dear to and revered by not only Liberals but all well disposed Canadian citizens. I refer to Sir Wilfrid Laurier. During the last days of his life he was present at a meeting of the Eastern Ontario Liberal Association, held in this city, and on the 14th January, 1919, he spoke as follows, concerning the trade question:
Sir, I told you at the commencement of my speech that it was the commercial freedom of England which enabled her to pass triumphantly through this war from an economic point of view. England, needless to say, has always been in the van of the greatest advances with respect to freedom of any kind, whether it be religious freedom, civil freedom, or political freedom; there are no people in the world today who have a greater degree of these liberties than have the English people or the Canadian p^ple. In the matter of commercial freedom, England has not only been well to the front, but has been very much in advance of any other people.
Discussing the question of the granting of preference to Great Britain and the Conservative party's objections thereto, he stated:
We do it (we grant the preference) because we are British subjects and because we believe in the principles of free trade. We believe also that it is for the good of the Canadian people that we should adopt that policy, and by that policy we stand to-day.
I adhere to this budget and support it because of this fact; that we had a great convention at Ottawa in 1919. We passed a trade plank in the platform which I consider is a sound plank for the people of this country and after we had passed

The Budget-Mr. McMaster
that trade plank the present Minister of Finance allowed his friends to nominate him as the leader of the Liberal party. I do not think for one moment that the present Minister of Finance would ever, after that platform was passed, have allowed his friends to place him in nomination had he not been in substantial agreement with that platform-I do not mean to say that he was prepared to cross every " t " and to dot every " i " of the platform -but in substantial agreement with the decisions reached at that convention.
Let me speak just a moment in conclusion-and I have delayed the House too long-concerning where we can get the money. It is a hard thing to get money for the state; it presents many difficulties, and there are many dangers in connection with it. I am going to refer the Minister of Finance to what he said on the 14th of March, 1919, in this House, as reported on page 484 of Vol. 1, of Hansard, of 1919:
But my hon. friends who are interested in tariff questions will bear me out in this, that when you increase the tariff on a class of goods that are made at home, not only do you get the increased duty which you collect at the customs house, but for every dollar that you collect at the customs house for increased duty, the consumer pays to the manufacturer two dollars which does not go into the public treasury.
It is towards those two dollars that I direct the attention of the Minister of Finance. I believe it will be found on investigation, in certain lines, the Canadian manufacturer occupies the field to such an extent that imports are negligible. I believe it will also be found that he has abused this privilege that the tariff has given him by watering his stock, by capitalizing the tariff against the taxpayers of this country. I should like to draw to the attention of the House two instances which came to my notice just the other day, and which were given me by a man in whom I have the utmost confidence, Mr. Isaac Pedlow, who was a valued member of this House during the last Parliament. He is a merchant in Renfrew. He was selling collars for 18 cents each, or three for fifty cents. His competitors were selling the same collars for 25 cents each, and he was refused by the manufacturer additional supplies of those collars. The manufacturer would not allow him to sell the collar at the price at which he wanted to sell it. That is an example of the tyranny of the trust.

Let me give the House another example, which will interest the ladies. It refers to silk stockings. The Niagara Maid Manufacturing Company manufacture a silk stocking which was sold to Mr. Pedlow at what averaged $1.37 i a pair. He put them on the market at a very fair profit to himself, at $1.75 a pair, or a profit of between 30 and 40 per cent. His competitors were selling these stockings at $2 a pair, and he was instructed by the selling agency of the mill that he could have no more of those stockings unless he was prepared to sell them for $2 a pair instead of $1.75. You say: "Should the attention of people be drawn to such trifling matters as these?" Yes, because these things show that, in many lines of primary necessaries of this country-I suppose silk stockings are not an absolute necessity of this country, although some people may think they are-it is not the ordinary trading rules which obtain; but by the control of the market, because manufacturers can do this under no other circumstances, the manufacturer is endeavouring to make of free merchants men who have to be, to a certain extent, his serfs, to do what he tells them. It is what Mr. Edward Porritt calls an example of the new feudalism, and the sooner we get away from that the better.

speechtext:
I am glad to know that he has, and he will have every help which the member for Brome can give him to accomplish that end.
Now, we come to the amendment. I will not read it, because it reminds me of a story of John Henry Pope, who came from that part of the province of Quebec which I have the honour to represent. In talking about something that was said, he exclaimed: " There ain't nothing to it," and that is all, with due respect to the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) that I can say about the amendment. What is it? It is just another example of the policy of " scold." It gets you nowhere because, what do they say? Are they blaming the Minister of Finance because he has not taken duties down? Not at all. They want him to put them up. There is not very much in the amendment; there is not a great deal to it. I sometimes am glaid, because I am a humane

The Budget-Mr. Good
man, that the members of the official Opposition are not living in the sixteenth century and are not of the female sex, because at that time they had an institution known as the " ducking pool " for common scolds, and I am afraid many of them would run a close risk of landing in that watery place.
What of the future? What has been the record of the Liberal party in the past? Can we depend upon the record of the Liberal party in the past to give promise that the Liberal party will be the great party of progress and freedom in the future, because the party of progress and freedom, by whatever name that party may be called, is going to rule this country in the future. The Liberal party has traditions. It has given to this country William Lyon Mackenzie, Louis Joseph Papineau, Baldwin, Lafontaine, and Papin. It has given to the country George Brown and Aime Antoine Dorion. It has given to the country Alexander Mackenzie, Edward Blake and Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I believe we should endeavour to be true to those great men of the past, and to see that we carry on the affairs of the Liberal party and of the country along the lines which they laid down.

I would include him; but alas for him, he joined a Union government. But he was in his time a great tribune of the people, and his voice and his name will never be forgotten while Canada remains. It would be, I say, a sad thing if the parties of progress were disunited. We have had an example in the old land of the effect of disunion amongst the parties of progress. We have had the independent Liberals, we have had the Labour party, largely animated by the same ideals, largely standing for the same principle, but kept apart by certain things, perhaps of secondary importance. I want to see in this country-I know I do; I know I speak for my electors, and I believe I speak for the rank and file of the Liberal party throughout this country-a Liberal party so truly Liberal that, under the broad folds of its banner, all people who love Canada, who love progress, who love liberty, who love equality, may find their proper place. That party must be free from all sinister influences. It must be strong in the confidence of the people. It must deserve the confidence of the people.
It must be guided, not by the fitful flare of expediency, but by the polar star of those Liberal principles which in the past have animated men of good will to bring about, upon this old world of ours, better conditions for the plain and common man.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would not ask the indulgence of the House were it not for the fact that there are some very -important considerations in connection with the present question under discussion which have not yet been placed before the House, and for this reason I am going to ask that indulgence in order that I may present those considerations.
First of all, however, I should like to say this:	I did hope for very much
more, in the direction of what would seem to me to be real progress, than is evident in the budget that has been proposed. And perhaps, if I were absolutely sincere, I might say that I did not expect very much more, knowing the record and the present composition of the so-called Liberal party. Regarding the amendment, I have nothing to say. But I have looked up the record of the Liberal party, both in the recent and remote past, in connection with the tariff question and the whole protective philosophy, and I shall present to the House a brief statement of the various opinions which have been proclaimed by the Liberal party for some little time in regard to this subject. In discussing the amendment, I think it is quite pertinent that we should know what the Liberal party has stood for, and what it purports to stand for at the present time.
Now, in regard to the last campaign, I would submit to the House-and I do so subject to correction by the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond)-that this hon. gentleman, at all events, did make it perfectly plain to his constituents that he did not subscribe to the 1919 platform of the Liberal party in respect to its tariff planks. How many other hon. members who proclaim themselves Liberals occupy the same position and so stated their attitude during the last Campaign I do not know, but I know that in this particular case the hon. member for Brantford proclaimed openly and publicly that so far as the tariff plank in the Liberal party's platform was concerned, he repudiated it.
Next, I want to refer to some history, and I shall begin with a little item that appeared in the Toronto Globe of April 15, 1858. It reads:
A meeting called by agreement of gentlemen holding protectionist views on commercial mat-
The Budget-Mr. Good

ters in various parts of the country assembled yesterday in St. Lawrence Hall in this city. The aggregate attendance was about two hundred.
That this meeting was attended with success is indicated in an item which appeared in The Globe of March 25th, in the next year, 1859. Note the following:
With a degree of haste as rare as it is unseemly, the government yesterday forced the new tariff through all its stages in the legislative council. It was read the first, second and third time on one day; and now only awaits the Governor^General's sanction to become law. To accomplish their purpose ministers proposed to set aside an established rule of the council devised to prevent precipitous legislation; and they succeeded in carrying the point.
I wish now to call the attention of the House to a number of addresses that were given in the campaign of 1877, published under this title:
Picnic Speeches Delivered in the Province of Ontario During the Summer of 1877, by the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie, the Hon. Edward Blake, the Hon, R. J. Cartwright, the Hon. L. S. Huntington, and the Hon. David Mills.
There is some interesting reading in this record of the position which the Liberal party took in regard to the tariff question at that time. I want to quote just one extract from the remarks of the Hon. David Mills:
"The Conservative opposition"-said Hon. David Mills, March 15, 1877, in denouncing customs duties-"might disguise their proposal as they please, but it meant plunder and nothing else. It meant taking from the pockets of every consumer a sum to be given to some other person; and the system by which this was done was a system of plunder".
"If", continued Mills, "people knew that honourable gentlemen opposite intended to impose taxes to the amount of twenty-eight million dollars instead of fifteen millions, and that only fifteen millions would go into the public treasury, the balance passing into the pockets of certain capitalists, they would not support such a proposal. And yet, that is precisely the proposal of honourable gentlemen opposite, disguise it as they may."
The next record which I shall submit to the House is from a speech of the late Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Speaking at the Liberal Convention in Ottawa, June 20-21, 1893, he said:
It seems to me that it (the Paterson resolution) could hardly be improved upon. It is a thorough arraignment of the policy the government has followed. It sets forth all the evils which have flowed from the system of protection. It draws the line, clear and distinct, between the policy of liberty and freedom, and the policy of slavery; because, I leave it to the judgment of every free man, to the farmers, and above all I leave it to the working man in the cities, if protection is anything else but slavery.
I have many other quotations in connection with that Liberal Convention of 1893.

I shall not read them all at the present time because it would take too long. But a number of statements were made by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and others; and there were statements as well embodied in the election literature issued by the Liberal party in the campaign that took place in 1896, I have one here from the handbook that was used at that time:
Protection has been tried and found wanting. The Liberals offer a policy of free trade limited only by the necessities of revenue required for the honest, economic administration of the Government.
In the platform of the Liberal party as adopted on that occasion we find a most sweeping condemnation of the whole protective system:	I have it before me, but
I shall not take time to read it. I wish, however, to remind the House of what happened in 1896; and although, I should like to feel a little more charitably disposed towards the government of that day than I do feel, at the same time I want to say frankly that it was a most bitter disappointment to the farmers- and shall I say ?-to very many other people in this country that, in the first revision in 1897 that followed the election of the new government, further reductions were not made in the tariff. And I must say that, looking back on the history and the record of the government of that time, and seeing the beginning which is now made in, I admit, the right direction, we wonder whether or not the history of that time and that government is to be repeated on this occasion.
Now, reference has been made to the election of 1911. I want to read a little item from the Toronto Globe of November 8, 1911. Commenting upon the situation that then existed and that had existed for some time previously, this paper said:
The big interests of all kinds in Canada, like their ilk in the United States, while as individuals they call themselves Liberals or Conservatives, and may even hold party offices, are not any longer in any real sense party men. Great railway corporations, protected monopolies, and the banks that finance their exploitations and mergers are playing in Canada the same bipartisan game that was played so disastrously to public interest and national honour in the United States. Let there be no mistake. The horns and hoofs of the American system are already within the doorstep of Canada's house of government. The fight for freedom from its vulgar and oppressive domination has only begun in Canada.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we know what happened in 1911. I supported the late Hon. William Paterson with all my strength in that election, and I have always be-

The Budget-Mr. Good
Iieved that the adoption of the Reciprocity Agreement would have been one of the best things that could have happened to this country. So I want to give every credit to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) and to his colleagues in the then government for their action at that time. But a year later we have a pronounce-' ment by a gentleman who now sits in this House as senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean). On March 13th, 1912, he stated:
We were divided in Canada on the National Policy for a good many years. Nevertheless, once the two parties came to see that the National Policy was essential to the country that division disappeared.
The hon. member was, I believe, an adherent of the Liberal party then in opposition, and here we have a frank admission that any difference which had existed between the two old parties prior to 1911 had then disappeared.
And I have another quotation here, Mr. Speaker. It is from a speech delivered in this House on June 9th, 1919, by a gentleman who announced himself as a protectionist Liberal. I refer to Hon. C. C. Bal->
lantyne, who was Minister of Marine and Fisheries in the late government. Listen to this, Sir:
I am a protectionist Liberal, a believer in moderate protection. Before I strayed from the fold, I did not find that my views were at variance with those of the majority of members composing the Liberal party of that day. Nor do I think that my views as a moderate protectionist Liberal would be much at variance to-day with those of the majority of hon. members sitting to the left of the Chair. We can only judge the Liberal party by the policy they pursued during the fifteen years they were in power. I for one saw no tangible signs of free trade during that period.
Mark that, Mr. Speaker:
I for one saw no tangible signs of free trade during that period.
An admission by a man who represented himself as belonging to the Liberal party, that he saw no signs of free trade, apparently no signs of the carrying out of the professions made in the platform of 1893, during those fifteen years from 1896 to 1911! I am not saying he is right, but that is his statement made on the floor of this House only two years ago. He continued :
The manufacturers of this country were perfectly satisfied with the fiscal policy of the Liberal government during those fifteen years . . . I think I may safely say that one can take as his very best guide in matters of this kind the policy of such great men as have filled the office of prime minister of this country during the last fifty years, and when the policy
of moderate protection has been adhered to by both Conservative and Liberal governments, that must be the easiest and best way of raising the necessary revenue, and also the fairest and most equitable system, having regard to the diversified interests that exist.
Then I have here the tariff planks in the Liberal platform of 1919, partly quoted in the amendment. I am not going to read those planks; we all know what they are. They practically reassert the assertions in the platform of 1893, and they are, as everyone knows, in very marked accord with the tariff planks in the Farmers' national platform.
Now, with respect to this extraordinary transformation-one authority has called it the " great apostacy "-I find the following in the report of the tariff committee of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association for 1918-19 as printed in Industrial Canada for July 1919:
As the tariff changes demanded at this session of Parliament-
That is 1919.
-go much farther than the Reciprocity Agreement of 1911 towards free trade with the United States, the threatened danger to the future of Canada is proportionately increased. Prom these denationalizing agencies our protective custom laws, inaugurated forty years ago, preserve our country. It is fundamental that the maintenance of our separate British nationality depends upon the retention of our freedom to shape our protective custom laws to serve our own needs.
In conclusion perhaps I might read a rather cynical comment which appeared in "Saturday Night" upon the situation as represented in the extract that I have just read. As I say, the comment is rather cynical, but it contains a good deal of wisdom. It is as follows:
The flag-waver is generally the man with the coin, or the man with the axe to grind. It was ever so. Kings and princes, through all the centuries, have waved their flags and their banners, and called upon their loyal supporters to fight the enemy. And the loyal supporters were just good enough and foolish enough to do it. Therefore, the kings and princes continued to rule over them and so they should. The financial kings and princes now wave the flag. The voter comes manfully forward and, with eyes blinded with patriotic tears, marks his little cross on the ballot for the "interests". Therefore the "interests" continue to rule over us, and so they should.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am going to ask a very definite and, I think, a fair question. What is the significance of the extraordinary variety and contradictory nature of the views expressed and the conduct of the Liberal party for the last fifty years? To me there are three possible explana-
The Budget-Mr. Good

tions: First, was the Liberal party insincere in its professions? If it was, that is an explanation. I do not answer the question; I ask it. Second, was it bribed, controlled or dominated against its convictions by tariff beneficiaries? Again, I do not answer that question; I ask it. Or third, has it honestly changed its mind and adopted protection as a sound national policy? I think that we who sit in this quarter of the chamber, at all events myself, have a right to ask those questions, and to have them answered. I am not going to answer them, because I cannot.

speechtext: Why not make it twenty-four hours, and not fifty years?

speechtext:
In that connection I am going to refer to some statements that were made here a few weeks ago, and one just the other day by some British Columbia members, to the effect that one's views on the tariff are geographically determined, and, further, that the whole tariff question is one of expediency and compromise and not one of principle. Even if it were true that one's views on these matters were determined by one's place of residence, the rightness or wrongness of the tariff system would not be thereby determined in the most infinitesmal respect. I would like to repudiate absolutely the suggestion that we in this chamber are morally justified in considering this question from the selfish standpoint of our own occupation or our own locality. It seems to me that if we cannot approach the question from the point of view of the general interests of Canada, then it is absolutely hopeless to fry to arrive at any right conclusion. I propose, therefore, to examine the protective system without any reference to locality or occupation and to ask the question:	Is
it a sound national policy? Were the professions of the Liberal party in times gone by, as stated in their platforms, based on sound principles, or were they not? I hope in that review and criticism of the protective philosophy to establish this point: viz, that the whole protective system has no possible justification from the point of view of right and justice.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
