subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
fact they must argue if they are logical, that the removal of the tariff wall from the western boundary of these two provinces to the eastern boundary was a misfortune. I think it must be evident to all hon. gentlemen that the protectionist reasoning breaks down when you consider that political boundaries are arbitrary and often shift overnight. Indeed, I believe that unhampered trade, if we would but once realize it, pays no more attention to political boundaries than do the birds of the air of the fishes of the sea.
I pass now to consider for a moment tariffs for revenue and tariffs for protection. Historically tariffs originated as means of securing revenue. I do not think there is any doubt about that; and a celebrated Frenchman, once speaking of this particular system, said that it was the best way of "plucking the goose with the least squawking."
It seems to me that the system which was thus described accords with a system of government which has very happily disappeared-a system of government in which the governors by hook or by crook obtained what money they could by any and all kinds of taxation from unwilling subjects. But now under our system of government we are not subjects of a ruler, we are citizens of a country, and if we have the proper point of view we contribute taxes willingly for the public services. And it seems to me that indirect taxes are bad in themselves largely because they are indirect, and that in this respect direct taxes are much better. Indirect taxes, like the tariff tax, the sales tax, and other like taxes, may be evaded, concealed and shifted, and often are, and the results are unfortunate.
Now, turning to tariffs for protection, I very frankly admit that it may seem to be in the public interest to protect certain infant industries for the time being. But I submit that if the collective wisdom of the people decides that any particular industry which has a fair prospect of becoming permanently self-sustaining needs assistance by the state, this assistance should be given directly in the form of a bounty, instead of indirectly by means of a tariff. In order to make my meaning clearer, I submit a base which I think will illustrate the difference between the bounty system and the tariff system from the purely protective point of view. Let it be supposed, for example, that we want to encourage the development of aerial navi-
gation. Would it be a sensible policy to assist the people engaged in that development by granting them a bounty, or by putting a handicap upon all other means of transportation-to put a tax upon the use of our highways, our railways and canals, and in that indirect way assist the infant industry of aerial transportation? It seems to me that when we look at it this way we see that the bounty or direct subsidy, if it be necessary, is in every way to be commended as compared with the indirect system of protection by means of tariffs, because under the bounty system you pay only in proportion as the particular industry which it is desired to develop does develop, and you do not put a handicap upon all other competing industries. I must say in that connection that while the bounties which were given a good many years ago by the government of which the present Minister of Finance was also then Minister of Finance may have been excessive, I do think that the principle then adopted to assist certain industries was the right principle, providing, of course, that assistance was considered necessary or advisable.
However, there is another consideration which I think we ought to bear in mind in connection with the so-called encouragement of infant industries, and that is that as soon as the infants get big they want more encouragement than when they were small. In a word, in practice, the system does not work out according to the theory. I suppose all farmers have observed that in litters of pigs the little runt, instead of getting the best place and the biggest share, is shoved off to one side by the big husky fellows, and he is practically starved to death.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The bigger the calf the more milk he takes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As one hon. gentleman remarks, the bigger the calf the more milk he takes-and, I think, the more anxious he is to stay on the job and the more fuss he makes when weaning time comes.
Now, Mr. Speaker, when we look back over the history of our protective system,
I think we shall find that these infants as soon as they grow pretty big shove the little fellows to the wall and continue to get the lion's share. So while it may be theoretically defensible to encourage infant industries, either by tariffs or bounties- and I think the bounty system is very much better; in fact, I think the tariff system is

The Budget-Mr. Good
indefensible-in practice the more encourag-ment they get the more they want. That has been the history of the encouragement of infant industries in this country, and I think it should bid us beware.
But some of the adherents of the protective system claim that we must have "adequate protection" of all Canadian industries. I submit that in the nature of the case this is impossible. You cannot protect local industries-a local newspaper, a local blacksmith, or any other local industry-their field is necessarily restricted, and therefore it is absolutely absurd to talk about protecting those industries. In the second place, you cannot protect those major industries which have a surplus to export, such as our wheat-growing industry in the Canadian West, our cattle industry, or any other of a number of our major industries-these it is impossible to protect. It is absolutely impossible to give adequate protection to all Canadian industries. It does not and cannot work out that way, and we have to recognize the fact that when we once start the system the inevitable result is that the few industries,- the big husky infants, so to speak,-get the lion s share and the (Others necessarily are left with the husks.
The protective system is also advocated as necessary to secure what is called a "favourable balance of trade". Now, if that is a desirable end in view, why should we not carry goods from where they are dear to where they are cheap? In that way we would get a maximum export and a minimum import. Or, better still, let us sink all ships at sea, and then we will have the summum bonum of the protectionist philosophy so far as it applies to international trade. I think the protectionist fails to see that international trade is essentially barter, and that in the long run imports and exports have to balance one another. This is a recognized truth amone economists, and we should not forget it. Of course, there are some modifications when one country pays tribute to another in the form of interest.
In regard to protection against what is called cheap foreign labour, the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) dealt with that this afternoon, and showed very conclusively I think that so-called cheap labour is not by any means always really cheap labour. The cost of production indeed is dependent not only on wages but on climate, on resources and on the efficiency of labour; and this we must bear in mind.' We should
also bear in mind in that connection the distinction between what we might call real wages and nominal wages.
I submit further, Mr. Speaker, that no matter what the advantages of one country may be over another, international trade is always beneficial, because in some respects one country will have certain relative advantages over its neighbours, and those industries in the one country which have a relative superiority will be able to export their produot to the other country. Let me take an example:	It might be argued thaf
we can manufacture sugar in Canada more cheaply than they can manufacture it in the West Indies, but I submit that even though that be true our advantage over the West Indies in the production of wheat and cattle is so marked that it is a better and more sensible policy for us to use our labour in those industries and buy our sugar from the West Indies, for instance, rather than manufacture it at home.
Now, in regard to retaliatory tariffs, it seems to me that this is something which comes home very strongly to a great many people. It is said that the United States has done us a bad turn; that they have been disagreeable; that they have been unfair, and the sentiment at once is to retaliate. If they will not let us into their market, it is argued, then we should not let them into ours. But I submit that if we take that attitude we are likely to cut off our nose to spite our face. When we look into the matter a little more closely we find that that policy is essentially a mistaken one. Take the case of two men, one specializing1 in the growing of wheat and the other in the growing of potatoes. It is a great advantage for the man who wants the excellent wheat to go to his neighbour and get it, and it is likewise an advantage to the man who wants the excellent potatoes to be able to get them from his neighbour. Suppose the wheat grower went to the other man and, upon endeavouring to sell his wheat to him, was met with refusal what would you think of him if he said: Well, if you will not buy my wheat, I will not buy your potatoes"? He would simply be denying him-self the advantage of getting the good potatoes which the other man was specially qualified to produce. It seems to me that if we eliminate sentiment in this matter and study it on a "common sense basis, we must admit that the policy of retaliatory tariffs is indefensible. The only passible justification I can see for it is that by threatening the other man or the other country you might bring him or



The Budget-Mr. Good
them to terms. I do not know how far that is possible; I am afraid, however, that the effect would be the opposite.
A good deal has been said about diversified industry. That is another claim which is made for protective tariffs; it is said that protection does secure diversified industries. I think that protectionists make an entirely unwarranted assumption in this regard. I do not think that tariffs are necessary to build up diversified industry in any country. In fact, I deny it abso-. lutely; all history and all common sense point in the other direction. Where you have a country opened up as our Northwest has been opened up in recent years, you will find the primary industries being first developed, and then when the proper time comes you will find, inevitably, the development of the secondary industries taking place. It is impossible for any civilization to develop unless in that particular way. While it may be possible to encourage certain secondary industries by tariff protection and by bounties, it is not necessary to enact tariff walls or adopt a protective system in order to secure diversification of industries.
I would like to submit in that connection also to some of our protectionist
9 p.m. friends in this chamber that at the present time the Canadian manufacturer, who has been crying out for protection for so long, finds his Canadian market practically gone on account of the decadence of agriculture. We heard yesterday from the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond) how the warehouses of the manufacturers of implements in the city of Brantford are full and the workmen idle. Why are they full? Because the farmers are in such a position at the present time that they cannot buy. I would like to submit to our manufacturing friends that they should turn their eyes a little more definitely to our Canadian market and endeavour to ascertain how the Canadian farmer can be advantaged, how he can be put in a position to buy their implements. I submit also to our protectionist friends that they should consider the possibility of developing an export trade. I cannot understand why the Canadian manufacturers, who are such agitators and propagandists for protective tariffs, do not see that if they are going to develop an export trade as have England, Belgium, Switzerland and the other countries we heard of yesterday and this afternoon, they have to reduce their cost of production in this country. That is the only pos-
[Mr. Good. 3
sible way in which they can compete in a foreign market in manufactured goods.
Personally, I wish our Canadian manufacturers all success and all prosperity; I would like to see Canadian manufacturing developed to a much greater extent than it is at the present time. But I contend that that can be done not by imposing protective duties, not by hampering both the primary and the secondary industries of the country, but by giving the manufacturer free raw material and lower labour costs-and we can give the Canadian manufacturer lower labour costs by making the cost of living lower for the Canadian working man. It seems to me, therefore, that a freer trade policy would be absolutely to the advantage of the Canadian manufacturers, as it has been for the British manufacturers. It would be to the advantage both of agriculture and of the primary and secondary industries.
It is said further that infant industries or small industries cannot establish themselves in the face of competition from the old established and stronger industries. That is the plea constantly made on behalf of certain Canadian industries-that they cannot compete against the larger industries in the United States. If that is true, Mr. Speaker, what of the manufacturing in our own West which is beginning to be established? Are these manufacturers able to establish themselves against the competition of the old established and stronger manufacturing industries in the Canadian East? We have no tariff between the Canadian West and the Canadian East. Would our protectionist friends advocate a tariff between western Canada and eastern Canada in order to protect the manufacturing industries in western Canada? I ask them, frankly and candidly, would they advocate that? It seems to me that if they are true to their own philosophy they must advocate a tariff in order to protect the infant manufacturing industries of western Canada against the older and longer established industries in the East.
I want to submit in this connection that if we study the industrial history of the United States we shall find that as the primary industries developed in the Mississippi valley and westward, the secondary industries followed them up and established themselves through that whole territory in oen competition with the long established manufacturing industries on the Atlantic sea-board. I remember some

The Budget-Mr. Good
years ago talking to a couple of men from the New England states who were interested in the boot and shoe industry. They told me that in St. Louis the boot and shoe industry had become firmly established in open competition with the very powerful boot and shoe industries in the New England states. Why? Because the market was out there, because the raw material was out there, and because the manufacturers saw the possibilities and the prospect of sure success in that territory. And so it will be everywhere: If we have concern for the development of our primary industries we do not need to worry about our secondary industries. They will follow when needed.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there is another consideration I would like to present to our protectionist friends and it is this: That protective tariffs cannot effectively protect unless they lead to monopoly; and why? Because under free competition all profits tend to a common level. If the profits in any particular business are inordinately large, and free competition is permitted, others will go into that particular line in order to reap those profits, and the only , way in which that can be prevented is by a combination to fix prices. And I submit to all hon. gentlemen here, that if we look back over the history of Canadian manufacturing for the- last thirty years, we shall see that under the cover of tariff protection, and in order to take full advantage of tariff protection, the various industries have merged and amalgamated so as to very effectively destroy competition, for the very simple reason that if competition remained they could not reap the advantages of the tariff. So they have combined, and we have had a tremendous growth in these giant mergers in Canada, as well as m the United States, during the last twenty-five years; we have indeed had monopoly conditions.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that monopoly conditions are absolutely intolerable to a free people. If we are going to have monopoly it must be public monopoly; private monopoly is absolutely indefensible.
A moment ago I asked the question: Has protection assisted manufacturing? I think I answered that in respect to manufacturing in the United States. I now ask it with respect to Canadian manufacturing: Has protection assisted Canadian manufacturing on the average? I claim it has not, and that it cannot, both as regards the home market for manufactured goods,- 155J
that is the primary industries,-and as regards the export trade, in both cases our Canadian manufacturers stand to gain very greatly by a different policy-of freer trade.
I must hurry on. I have just one more point which I think it is worth while to emphasize in this examination of the protectionist system and it is this: There is, I think, no system that, from the standpoint of public morality, is more absolutely corrupting,-demoralizing and indefensible. I think that any system which opens the door for all and sundry to feed at the public trough, in a disgusting, corrupting scramble for special favours, is indefensible. I have had that admitted to me by protectionists-that there is a tremendous amount of wire pulling, lobbying and efforts to get special favours; and in that connection we find, I think in fact it has been pretty well admitted in Canada, that those concerned in it are people who expect, and have reasonable ground for expecting, that any investment in campaign funds will secure the retention for them of special privileges. It seems to me that there is no in-aictment against the protective system, more crushing, more damnable, than this' particular indictment that I have mentioned -that it has corrupted the public life of this country, and that it must corrupt the public life of any country where that system exists.
There is just one other thought that I would like to add. If the protectionist is driven, as I think he can be, by resistless logic, from one position to another, I have found in my experience that he takes refuge m this final stronghold. He says: National existence, national integrity is to be preserved above all things. National prosperity is of secondary importance; and he goes on to say, that in order to guarantee national ^ existence and national integrity, the nation must build up within itself practically all the industries that are necessary for the pieservation of that nation in time of war and that, no matter at what sacrifice, we must build up a completely diversified industry in the country, so that m time of war we shall be able to have everything that is necessary within our own boundaries: It is the ideal of national, economic self-sufficiency.
That claim, I think, ought to be met. It is fairly stated, and I would like to meet the claim as fairly and honestly as I can. It seems to me tfiat there are two fatal defects about ,that argument
The Budget-Mr. Good

__an argument which admits that the pro-*
tective system is impoverishing to a country, but which defends it on the ground that it enables a nation, in time of war, to maintain its integrity and existence.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that there are two fatal defects to that reasoning. In the first place it is not a practicable means of se-uring safety, particularly at the present time. We do not know what may he the methods of warfare in the future. We may strive as best we can, and exercise all the ingenuity of which we are capable; and yet when the next war comes we may find something that we had not thought of and provided for which would be the key to the whole question and would determine our fate for weal or woe. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that from that point of view the argument that we can establish national economic self-sufficiency falls down.
In the second place, while it is not a practicable means of securing safety, I do not believe if it were practicable that it would be right, for this reason-that it is not feasible for the smaller countries m any degree whatever. It may be measurably feasible for such countries as the United States, a country with most varied resources of all kinds. A country like the United States can attain, in a measurable degree, national economic self sufficiency. u take countries like Belgium, or Holland or Denmark-particularly Holland-the natural resources are so extremely limited that it is absolutely absurd to talk of economic self sufficiency. To recommend a policy of that sort for a country like Holland or Belgium is absolutely absurd and every one knows it-in fact any attempt by the people of Holland to attain national self sufficiency would be doomed to utter failure. Therefore, it seems to me that as in the Great War we sacrificed blood and treasure in order to protect the existence and integrity of small nations, we are not justified now in defending a policy which, for the small nations-no matter how feasible it may be for the large nations-is absolutely impracticable. I submit, therefore, that in the case of the smaller nations confidence must be reposed in the League of Nations idea, and in international trade.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am going to ask a question, just in conclusion, and it is this: If the case against protection is so overwhelming why is it not more apparent? Why do we, in spite of the logic of the situation, find such a strong feeling and

sentiment in favour of protection? I think there are	reasons for it.	The first
reason is that we find public opinion and public ideas warped and distorted by powerful selfish interests. In that connection I have a little extract from a book entitled "Democracy after the War" by s very eminent English economist, J. A Hobson. I will read what he says as to why the protective policy continues to receive so much public support, and I hope this will sink into the minds of some of oui protectionists friends. He says:
The explanation lies in the opposition between the interests of certain classes within each nation and the welfare of the nation as a whole, and in the ability of these classes to impose their class interests upon the statecraft of their country. Protection is a bad policy for a nation. It diminishes its total output of wealth, distributes it unfairly, imposes a secret, onerous and wasteful method of taxation, breeds political corruption, establishes monopolies and provokes illwill and quarrels with other nations. But it is a good policy for capitalists in certain well organised industries, who, by their political pressure can frame a tariff that enables them to raise their prices and increase their profits at the expense of the weaker industries, and the consuming Public. A part of the illicit profits which it yields can be applied to maintaining and enforcing the political pull and to spreading a propaganda representing protection as a sound national and imperial policy. The ill-will which tariffs beget in surrounding nations and the reprisals they evoke go to feed the delusion that trade is fundamentally a form of competition, not of co-operation, and that nations are hostile competitors. The diplomatic and sometimes the military conflicts which ensue from tariff wars confirm this delusion. So protection passes from the position of an unscrupulous scheme of class plunder into that of a patriotic public policy. Finally, given favouring circumstances, it can be rivetted upon the state as a political and military necessity. For states which stop the natural courses of trade with neighbours, cripple their development, "steal" their markets, and otherwise inflict economic injuries, live in fear lest the injured interests in these neighbour states may be strong enough to coerce their governments into forcible intervention. Given a group of powerful states, each controlled in its fiscal and its foreign policy by strong business interests, it is easy to perceive that a generally dangerous situation emerges. Each state, considering the possibility of invasion on the part of a foreign power or group of powers, must look not merely to its forcible but to its economic defences. So a national economy of industrial, agricultural and commercial selfsufficiency assumes the guise of a, vital policy, and permanent protection is established as its chief instrument. Under these conditions protection becomes an essential feature of national defence, an economic militarism."
That, Mr. Speaker, is one explanation of why it is that the protective philosophy continues to get so much support. In that connection, I would like to refer to an

The Budget-Mr. Good
editorial which appeared in the Montreal Witness some time ago, entitled "Where is the Consumer."? I shall not read it, but it says, as the hon. member from Brome (Mr. McMaster) remarked this afternoon, that the consumers are not organized to protect themselves. The producers in this line and that line are organized to protect themselves by exploiting the consumers throughout the whole country, and that is exactly in line with the statement which I have just read from Mr. Hobson. I have here a book which was sent to me some little time ago, published by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, entitled "The Tariff, why Canada needs It." This is part of the propaganda which these illicit gains give rise to, in order to persuade the Canadian people to maintain this system. I will read one or two sentences out of this book, to show the kind of logic that that association foists upon the Canadian public. On the first page of this book I find the following paragraph :
The objects of a protective system in Canada have been and should continue to be: (1) to diminish, as far as possible, the importation of goods from foreign countries which can be produced at home.
Mark the words "which can be produced at home." Now, we can produce oranges at home, we can produce bananas, and all kinds of tropical fruit. We can grow cotton at home. Would the Canadian Manufacturers' Association advocate that as a sensible national policy? It seems to me the statement is absolutely absurd, and that, in order to make a sensible reasonable statement, we have to insert the word "profitably" and make it read "profitably produced at home." If we insert the word "profitably" I subscribe to the statement, but that opens the whole question as to what industries we can profitably follow and encourage, and what we must leave for other countries to develop, because of their climate and conditions.
The second object, as here defined, reads:
(2)	To facilitate the importation of raw materials which cannot be produced at home.
Now, how, in the face of all that is reasonable and sensible, can the Canadian Manufacturers' Association come before the Canadian public and advocate a tariff to facilitate importation? We all know that, to facilitate importation, all we have to do is to put articles on the free list and admit them as freely as possible, I submit,
therefore, that this object, as stated here, cannot be in any way served by the imposition of tariffs. The third object is:
(3)	To encourage the exportation of Canadian materials as finished products.
We are all desirous of encouraging exportation, but how can we possibly encourage exportation by putting on tariffs and customs duties on imports? In order to facilitate exportation, we have, as I said a few minutes ago, to make manufacturing and production in this country as cheap as possible. If we want our exportation to be large, we must help all the industries in Canada to produce as cheaply and freely as possible, and, in order to do that, we must admit goods freely.
The fourth object, as here defined, reads:
(4)	To make Canada self-contained, by developing and encouraging within her boundaries all legitimate activities that will give occupation to her people.
* I am in accord with that. "All legitimate activities"-that is all right, but how is that accomplished by imposing tariffs? By imposing customs duties we encourage all kinds of illegitimate activities in Canada. We divert labour from activities that are native to the soil, and can be carried on profitably, to industries that are not indigenous, that have to be subsidized, and that can only be carried on at a loss. The fifth object as stated here is:
(5)	To secure revenue.
We all know that the tariff, as a means of securing revenue, has lamentably fallen down. It is true we secure a revenue from the tariff, but there are other ways of securing revenue. As far as protection is concerned, the higher we protect the less goods come in, and the less revenue we get on our imports. If these are the best reasons that the Canadian Manufacturers' Association can advance on behalf of the protective system, it seems to me they had better, as we say, "go back home and sit down."
I am going to ask another question in connection with the protective system in Canada. I have tried to show that it cannot be defended on any kind of national or international ground. The policy seems to me, from the standpoint of economics, to be indefensible. I ask a further question: How has it worked out in Canada? Well, as we all know, Canada is a young country, and a country of illimitable natural resources, and I do not know that there is any country on the face of the earth which to-day offers greater
The Budget-Mr. Good

opportunities for labour than Canada. We have for years followed a persistent immigration policy, trying to attract into Canada all kinds of people from abroad. How has it worked out? During forty years we have had this protective system in Canada, and I have here an examination of the growth in population during the various decades from 1871 to the present. I am going to give the House a summary of these results; it will not take very long to do so. In the decade from 1871 to 1881, that was before the establishment of the National Policy in 1878, I find that the net loss, after taking into consideration natural increase and immigration, was nil. (I may say that I have these figures from the Bureau of Statistics, and I believe they are substantially accurate.) In the next decade, from 1881 to 1891, I find that the net loss, after taking into consideration natural increase (and immigration, was 559,000. In the next decade, from 1891 to 1901, the net loss was 349,000. In the next decade from 1901 to 1911, the net loss -and these figures are more accurate as we go on, because we have more accurate records-was 703,000, and in the next decade, from 1911 to 1921, the net loss was considerably over 1,000,000. When we take into consideration with that the most deplorable depopulation in our rural districts and the condition of agriculture in Canada, and when we realize that, during the last four decades, under a protective system, there has been a steady draining of people away from this great new country of Canada with all its resources, I think we must realize that that constitutes a moist terrific indictment against the protective policy, because, in this country we cannot hold the people that come here, if they are coming in and going out again, that surely indicates that there is something wrong with conditions. It is not Canada; Canada is all right; it is the laws we have enacted which have made it difficult in this country to develop our natural resources. A little over a year ago there was placed before the Tariff Commission by the educational secretary of the United Farmers of Ontario, a statement in which he summed up the effect of the protective system of Canada in this way:
1.	It has not eliminated the possibility of unemployment.
2.	Protection has failed to maintain a remunerative market for farm produce.
3.	Proteotion has failed to maintain a favourable trade balance.
IMr. Good.]
4.	Most disquieting of all perhaps, the protective tariff has failed to prevent the spirit of unrest.
On the other hand these are some things that the protective system does:
It places the government under the necessity of maintaining a self-contradictory policy.
That is a tariff for revenue and a tariff for proteotion.
Protection affords a shelter behind which incompetent manufacturers and lazy manufacturers can .make a living at the expense of the consumer.
Lastly, the protective tariff directly fosters class organisation and class selfishness.
Therefore, the protective philosophy and the protective system absolutely fall down, I contend, from the standpoint of economics and from the standpoint of actual accomplishment and results in Canada. Prior to the war we had this economic industrial sickness prevalent in Canada, a serious economic condition, due, I submit, to mistaken policies. I think .that sickness was aggravated by the war, because while, during the war, as Sir Thomas White has maintained, the war was largely paid for by extra work and extra sacrifice on the part of the Canadian people, at the same time, we permitted, we even encouraged, war profiteering, and then I think, even worse than that, we permitted many of the profiteers to salt down their unholy gains in Dominion bonds, some of them untaxable. Worse than that, deflation has come, and we find that these Dominion bonds will have to be redeemed with double value, either in service or commodities, by the Canadian people.
It is true that during war time, various expedients were resorted to in order to increase the revenue, because at that time, as all hon. gentlemen will remember, the tariff tax fell lamentably short. Besides that, in some of these expedients, there was a dim perception that those who had enriched themselves by a protective tariff and war profiteering, should shoulder a larger share of the burdens. Some of the expedients that were resorted to in war time were as follows: The excess profits tax, the income tax, the stamp tax, the luxury tax, the sales tax and so on. But with all these expedients we find to-day that the country is steadily going into debt. Industry is paralyzed, the farmers are discouraged and production is stagnant.
Just in connection with one of the various expedients that were adopted during war time, I want to submit a little in-

The Budget-Mr. Good
formation, which, perhaps, will explain to the House why it is that, in some respects at least, we have not got better results.
I refer to the excess profits tax. Some little time ago, I asked a question which stood upon the Order Paper in this House for a long time. Finally, it was evaded; it was not answered. I may say that this question was based on certain information that I had received privately, and I want now to submit to the House that information without mentioning any names. A certain company in a certain year had a capital stock, according to this statement, as follows: $250,000; reserves, $731,350.20, making a total capital employed of $981,350.20. The gross profit of that company, according to the statement submitted, was, I am told, $1,571,626.17. Deducting from that the income tax

I will not read the figures; I have them here-the decrease in the inventory and the depletion, I find there is left a net profit of $1,423,764.31. According to the act, I am informed that the assessment levied on that company in that particular year should have been $1,111,983.99, made up as follows: 7 per cent of the capital employed, exempt from taxation; 8 per cent, one-quarter taken by the government; 5 per cent, of capital employed, one-half taken by the government and of the balance of profits, which was considerably over $1,000,000, six-sevenths should have come into the federal treasury. The total assessment which, according to this statement, ought to have beeen levied on that particular company, was considerably over $1,000,000. What was the actual assessment by the department?- $214,312.36. In connection with this one company for one year, if these figures are correct, and if there is no good justification for the action which the department has taken, there is an apparent loss to the country of $897,671.63!
There is a situation which I think calls for some inquiry. I submit it to the House because I asked questions based on the information that came to me privately, and I got no answer. I think that if that sort of thing has been happening in Canada and we have not got millions of dollars of excess profits that we were entitled to receive during and since the war, we should know the reason why.
But in spite of all these expedients to which we have resorted, the country has been steadily going into debt. We have been discussing for days now the unfortunate railway situation that Canada finds herself in, the unfortunate condition of agriculture, and the paralysis of the manufacturing industries. There is no industry in this country that has not been deploring its condition; and yet, in the face of all these things, the first budget of a new Government proposes nothing but the same old nostrums. And I say that in all charity. There is not a glimmer even of anything new; there is no promise of relief; there is only the pathetic, tragically blind clinging to the past. Thus it hath been, thus it ever shall be.
I stated at the outset that I was keenly disappointed with the budget, and I am. I should not be so disappointed if there were any inkling in it of anything of a radical nature to which we might look with hope for the future; and it is because I do not see in it anything of a constructive, radical character that holds out some promise of relief in the future that I am going to present to the hon. members of this House something of a different nature which it seems to me does promise very considerable relief. And in order to approach the question in a logical and systematic way, I shall ask, first of all, this question: What is a just system of taxation? To answer that question we must ask another. What is taxation for? Are not taxes contributions by individuals for the purpose of carrying on collective or community undertakings? Are they not payments by the individual to the community in return for services rendered the individual by the community? I think they are; and I hope that that is a fair statement of what taxation is for. For instance, we have in our municipalities, schools, streets, and so forth, which are maintained by taxation; and we have in our Dominion, railways, canals, and other public utilities which are kept up in the same way. From this point of view, let us examine the various kinds of taxes which are levied in Canada. We can classify these taxes under three general heads.
In the first place, we have a tax on consumption, the tariff tax, the sales tax, etc. As has already been abundantly shown in this debate, this tax as levied on the necessaries of life bears hardest on those who are least able to pay, namely, the average man with the large family. I am well aware that the member for one of the Bruces, I think (Mr. Malcolm), said yesterday that the rich man paid in proportion to his riches through the sales tax. I submit, however, that that is not so. This particular tax, especially as it
The Budget-Mr. Good

applies to the necessaries of life, falls upon the average man with a large family much more heavily than it does upon the rich man. Moreover, it is in no sense proportionate to the services rendered the individual by the community. Let me take an example to show that. Suppose a bachelor to be the owner of a valuable mining property, yielding him, say, a million dollars a year without any effort on his part. Now, I happen to know one man-he is not a bachelor, but I do not think he has any children-who wais very much in that position some years ago. He received an enormous income, although I do not know that he got quite as much as I have suggested. I think, however, that this is a fair supposition. We will suppose that he gets a million dollars a year by reason of his ownership of this valuable property. Now, then, imagine one of his employees working for $3 a day and having to support a family of five. That employee may pay, indeed, will pay, more for the necessaries of life than the rich bachelor who is in receipt of a million dollars a year without any effort on his part. That is about the way the sales tax and the tariff tax work out.
Or take another example. In western Canada the Canadian Pacific Railway has been granted by the Canadian people quiet possession of thousands of square miles of valuable land which is increasing in value by reason of the labour of neighbouring settlers, while those settlers pay heavy customs and sales taxes on all their supplies. I think that is an outrageous, a scandalous state of affairs. So far as the ownership of that property is concerned, the Canadian Pacific Railway pays not one cent of taxation into the federal treasury, while the people who are settled in these districts pay heavy customs and sales taxes on all the commodities they require. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the tax on consumption is unjust and unwise and should be abolished, perhaps not immediately, but as soon as may be. There is one exception, possibly, which I would make. If it is considered desirable to discourage the use of any commodity, then the customs tax or the sales tax would be justifiable. If we could only agree on what commodities are to be discouraged, then of course we might permit a heavy tax to remain on them. But the difficulty is that we cannot agree on this point; some commodities are felt to be useful to one man while they are a curse to another, 
and we cannot find any common basis for action in regard to most commodities which we call luxuries. There are some, perhaps, like alcoholic beverages, which we would generally agree should be taxed under this system. But even if we could agree that customs duties and sales taxes are proper and wise on such commodities, I am afraid we should not get a very large revenue from taxes of this kind.
The second species of tax I desire to refer to is exemplified in the graduated income and inheritance taxes. The basis of these taxes is the "ability to pay"; but the ability to pay is not always a measure of the privileges, rights, and services conferred upon or rendered to the individual by the community. Perhaps under existing conditions it is largely so, but there are notable exceptions. Take the case of two farmers living side by side on land of equal natural value and equal value so far as location is concerned. One farmer may be diligent, enterprising and thrifty and may do well. He may accumulate quite a competence, build up his farm, and in the course of some years develop a very valuable property. The other man may be lazy, thriftless, and live on the verge of bankruptcy practically all the time. This, I think, must indicate to us that it is not always wise to tax according to ability to pay. In this particular case it is grossly unfair. Both these men nave equal opportunities so far as the community is concerned, though perhaps the poor, ignorant, lazy man might claim that society owed him better care when he was a youngster than to bring him into a condition of that sort. But leaving that aside, I do not think we should penalize thrift and industry, as we are bound to do in a tax based exclusively upon ability to pay. Industry ought to be encouraged; and if we permit idleness to eat the bread of industry, then by and by we are not going to have very much bread in this country.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this is one of the most important questions which we have to consider in connection with taxation. We must, I believe, devise a system of taxation which does not discourage but which encourages industry. Now, if, as in some of these cases I have mentioned, the idler gets the biggest return, and the worker has to labour hard for a pittance, we are certainly not doing very much to encourage thrift and industry; and I submit that the whole system

The Budget-Mr. Good
of taxation on consumption and to some extent that according to "ability to pay" has the effect of discouraging thrift and industry and encouraging idleness.
However, while making that statement, I do think that the apportionment of taxation according to ability to pay is largely justified nowadays, because by unjust systems of taxation and by other special privileges we have allowed the idler to confiscate the earnings of the worker. Having permitted the poor to be robbed-and in this connection I recall a rather well-known phrase of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, "Protective tariffs are legalized robbery" -having permitted the poor to be robbed, we make a belated and largely futile effort to recover part of the spoils, and, unfortunately, in so doing we incidentally penalize honest industry and thrift. I think it would be better to purify the stream at its source, to stop the iniquity at the beginning.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the hon. member will allow me, he has made it abundantly plain that he is altogether opposed to a protective tariff. If in power would he by one stroke sweep away all tariffs, or would he get rid of them gradually?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can answer my hon. friend's question definitely and honestly. I would not advocate the sweeping away of all protective duties immediately. I would set about discovering some better system of taxation and introduce that gradually to replace what I regard as a vicious system.
Now, the third system or species of taxation is exemplified, although but imperfectly, in the ordinary property tax. Property in common usage comprises many essentially different things: land, mines, water-powers, buildings, tools, clothing and everything else to which exclusive legal right is given the individual by the state. But of these various kinds of property there are two main classes: first, those kinds of property which are not the product of labour, such as unimproved farm land, mineral resources, water-powers, site values, etc.; and, secondly, those kinds of property which are the product of labour such as wheat, houses, clothing, tools, etc. The first class is designated in the platform of the Progressive party as "unimproved land values, including all natural resources;" and the broad and vital distinction between the two classes of property can be well summed up in the terms, "land values" and "labour values"; and
the Farmers' platform, as is well known, advocates the taxation of land values.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I submit that there is no juster or more accurate measure of the rights, privileges and services conferred upon the individual by the state than the land values to which he has legal title under our existing laws, for the ground rent of such land values is the measure thereof. This ground rent is the annual value of the rights, privileges and services conferred upon the individual by the state, because it can be enjoyed without personal effort on the part of the individual. Therefore the Progressive party advocates the taxation of land values for federal purposes, as they are now partly taxed for municipal and provincial purposes. I submit that the taxation of land values is based upon equity and justice, and, moreover, will have the incalculable advantage of stimulating instead of restricting and curtailing production.
We have been debating for many days how we are going to increase production in order to pay our enormous national debt and solve our railway problem. There is nothing more necessary in Canada from a material point of view than increased production. If we can solve that problem then we can solve our national debt and railway problems. Now, taxes on consumption, tariff and sales taxes, inevitably tend to curtail and discourage production; but taxation of land values has the opposite effect because it tends to force all natural resources to be used. To the prospective farmer it makes land cheaper, and thus decreases his cost of production. The substitution of the taxation of land values for the tariff and sales taxes, at least so far as necessaries are concerned, will reduce to the farmer both the cost of land and also the cost of supplies, and thus stimulate production. It will increase the average ability to pay, for all taxes come out of the wealth produced by those who labour, and anything which assists production to that extent increases the fund from which taxes come.
I do not think there is anything that we can turn our attention to of greater importance at the present time than this means of increasing production. And while the initial effect of this species of taxation would be to give every possible encouragement to the user of agricultural and other natural resources, it would have the secondary effect of increasing the value of these resources, and therefore increasing
The Budget-Mr. Good

the revenue which we derive by taxing them.
So far as our farmers are concerned, I made a calculation a few years ago as to the effect which the change resulting from substituting the taxation of land values in Ontario for the tariff tax would have on the farmers of that province, and I found that they would pay only one-tenth as much under the system of taxation of land values as they have been paying under the tariff system. That surely would be an immense inducement to farmers to speed up production. It would, I submit, assist very materially in the development of the most important of our primary industries.
In that connection I wish to point out again what has been pointed out so many times in the past, that the taxation of land values is not the taxation of land acreage or area. I think that those who go into the matter closely will find that in our agricultural districts unimproved land values are very, very small, and that this particular kind of taxation will be very easy on farmers. However, I do not think the farmer would be justified in supporting it on that ground-not at all, but on the ground that it is a system of taxation which is absolutely fair and just to all industries, and which is based upon the principle that taxation ought to be in proportion to the service rendered by the community to the individual.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I submit this question: Is the taxation of land values feasible, and what can we expect to get from it? Well, we have it to some extent municipally at the present time. We have in our municipalities all the machinery for assessing and collecting it so far as municipal values are concerned. We have it provincially in respect to the western surtaxes on vacant land, and we had it in Ontario in a measure during the war, when a limited amount of taxation was imposed by the province upon real estate for war purposes. We have it exemplified at the present time most completely by the Toronto Harbour Commission which has control of the " made land " along the Toronto waterfront. I understand that all that land is to be leased on short term leases and never sold. That policy which the Toronto Harbour Commissioners have adopted is almost a complete realization of the taxation of land values. Personally I am very glad indeed to see such an apparently successful and commendable example of this particular kind of taxation in the

municipal field. We have also in the Australasian countries-New Zealand and Australia-I have some particulars here, but I will not submit them to the House- we have a record of the taxation of land values for their federal purposes. Now, in regard to the taxation of land values for federal purposes, I am going to suggest to the hon. Minister of Finance that so far as municipalities are concerned, the machinery for assessment and collection is all there; no new machinery needs to be created; there is little added expense in utilizing the machinery already in existence. So far as the larger corporations and values are concerned which are not within	any	particular munici-10 p.m.	pality,	we	have already theincome	tax	machinery whichcan	be	employed	in	that connection. I
submit that we may very well begin to adopt a policy in that direction in the very near future-at once, even, and with pactically no expense for the creation of new machinery.
Now, what revenue can we expect this tax to give us? I made some calculations a few years ago regarding the unimproved land values in Canada, and while there was a good deal of guesswork about it, the conclusion I came to was that, roughly a one per cent tax on the unimproved land values of Canada would give us a revenue of $80,000,000. Now, that certainly is worth while, and if we begin in that little way, pretty soon, I think, we would find our financial burden very much lessened. I repeat the answer which I gave to the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Ryckman); I would not suggest any very drastic and sudden changes in our methods of taxation, but I would suggest the immediate beginning of something that is likely to become permanently valuable for this country. I see no difficulty about adopting this plan at once, assessing and collecting through our municipal machinery those values that lie within the municipalities, and assessing and collecting the tax on the other values through our income tax machinery. I submit that suggestion to the Minister of Finance, with every emphasis which I can possibly place upon it.
There are only two other suggestions, Mr. Speaker, which I wish very briefly to place before the Minister of Finance in regard to our whole financial situation. The first is this: that we might adjust

The Budget-Mr. Low
federal taxation and public works to prevent inflation and deflation. It is generally admitted that these booms and depressions occur in cycles and that during a period of inflation there is what you might call intoxication of industry. Prices go up; everybody thinks that prices are going to get better, and we have a period of inflation. Then the crest of the wave is reached, and we have a sudden drop- a slump. People get discouraged; we have paralysis of industry. We have such a situation now existing in Canada, aggravated of course, as it is at present, by the European situation. But, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that if the federal government were to levy heavier taxation during a period of inflation and withdraw money from circulation-not put it in the banks where it will go back again to stimulate industry; industry does not need stimulation at those times; it needs checking-. if such money as is not needed for the requirements of the time can be withdrawn from circulation and set aside for use in a period of deflation, we would have a sort of automatic control over the rising and falling of prices. When the period of deflation begins to come and men are thrown out of employment, we would have our public works to fall back upon.- works which had been held in suspension, so to speak. In that way a great deal of the distress which now prevails could be avoided. It seems to me this is entirely in line with the policy that any sensible farmer would follow. In a period of active demand for his crops, he would concentrate his energies upon raising crops to supply the demand, and then in a period of depression, having set aside some money for duller times, he would use the money and use his labour for the carrying on of certain improvements which he had delayed. If we could adopt a policy like that in our federal taxation we could in many ways prevent these recurring periods of depression-not, perhaps, entirely prevent them, but assist in controlling the situation, assist in preventing the serious evils that have arisen in that connection and which exist at the present time.
Just in conclusion, I want to suggest to the House that the whole question of the control of credit, which forms the subject of a resolution that was presented here some time ago, is a matter which should be studied very seriously by the Government in connection with our financial situation, and particularly in connection with the Bank Act, which is to be revised next year.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have perhaps taken more time than I had intended to occupy in presenting these views to the House, but I feel that I am justified, because these views have not, so far as I know, yet been presented to the House. They deal with part of the farmers' platform -the taxation of land values as a permanent policy of taxation. I submit that we should get away as soon as possible from the onerous and unfair methods of taxation which we have been following in the past and try to devise and adopt and apply a righteous system which will inevitably result in increasing the prosperity of this country.
Hon. THOS. A. LOW (South Renfrew) : Mr. Speaker, at this late hour I do not propose to occupy the time of this House at great length. But before I proceed I should like to extend to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) my most hearty congratulations upon his being spared to present his sixteenth budget. I know of no man in the public life of this country who enjoys the confidence of the people to a greater degree than the hon. Minister of Finance.
It occurs to me, Mr. Speaker, that the budget is very much like the financial statement of a great corporation as presented by its president. From that point of view I venture to make a few remarks to-night. While I have enjoyed the oratory of my hon. friend from Brant (Mr. Good) he will pardon me if I do not attempt to follow his remarks. The only thing I can say is that I thank Providence for having placed and kept men with the tariff views that my hon. friend entertains in the minority.
It will be generally admitted, Mr. Speaker, that when the present Government assumed office it was confronted with very serious problems, such as falling revenues and increasing expenditures, general business depression, and increasing unemployment. That the Government has met the situation in a fearless manner and has accomplished much will be admitted by the average citizen of Canada who is not unduly biased. I am sure that the action of the ministers of the various departments in their endeavour to reduce the expenditures of this country will commend itself to the people, as will also the statement made by the Minister of Finance that he intends to keep the
The Budget*-Mr. Low

expenditures within the revenue. The introduction by the Minister of Finance of new taxes that will bear as lightly as possible on the plain people of Canada will, I am sure, meet with general approval.
We all know that the tariff question has been the football of all political parties for the last fifty years. There are those who would abolish the tariff altogether as a cure for all our national ills. I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that I do not agree with that view, and that I do not think the farmers, of the province of Ontario at least, entertain any such opinion. I come from a constituency which is at least 60 per cent rural, and I want to tell hon. gentlemen that I received in the rural sections of that constituency almost as many votes as did the farmer candidate. Not because I told them that I would help them to escape the payment of a few dollars on agricultural implements. No; but because I told them that from my place on the floor of this chamber, and at all times, I would endeavour to secure for the farmers of this country better markets for the products they had to sell.
Now, Sir, in the province of Ontario I believe that the farmers, just the same as the urban portion of the population, if left to themselves would appreciate the value of a tariff. Why? Because they know that the best market they have is the home market; and I cannot understand how men argue from an opposite standpoint. Take a glance at the statistics for the year 1921, and what do we find? That the value of the total products of Canadian farms amounted to $1,396,233,000. After listening to the various speakers on the Progressive side you would imagine that the farmers received no benefit from the home market; that the market for their products was largely the export market. But what do we find? That in the same year, 1921, the total of farm products exported from this country amounted to $388,237,000. What does that mean? It means that the people of this country consumed 73 per cent of the products of every description produced on the farms of Canada, and that only 27 per cent was exported. I ask any fair minded member of this House if he would do anything to jeopardize the market that consumes 73 per cent of what the farmers produce.
We hear a great deal about the agricultural implement industry, and one would think from the arguments advanced that if the duty were completely removed from agricultural implements the farmers of this

country would be greatly benefited. But I find on referring to departmental records that the farmers in the Dominion of Canada purchased agricultural implements to the value of $51,637,441. Now admitting for the sake of argument that the manufacturers take advantage of the full benefit of the duty-which I do not admit-what would that mean to the individual Canadian farmer? According to last available figures there were 714,646 citizens engaged in farming. It would represent a per capita payment of $9.04. Yet some men tell us that the tariff is a great burden to the farmers, and that for the sake of saving $9.04 per capita they would wipe out one of the largest industries of our country, an industry that in the city of Toronto gives a living to at least one-twentieth of its entire population. Surely, if the farmers themselves had to vote on the question of killing an industry of that size they would hesitate about doing it. My opinion is that if the facts were plainly placed before them, they would stand by a policy that will build up the national industries of Canada, because they know that the better the home market is the more advantageous it is for our agriculturists.
I promised my constituents that if elected I would urge upon the Government of the day that negotiations be opened up with any country that would give us better markets for our agricultural products, and I am glad that I did not have to wait very long after coming to Ottawa to see that idea carried out. I found the Minister of Finance ready and willing to go to Washington to negotiate, if possible, a treaty that would be solely in the interests of the farmers of this Dominion. In 1911, although a manufacturer, I stood upon the floor of Parliament and urged the adoption of the Reciprocity Pact. Why? Because I believed then, as I believe now, that it wouldl not hurt the manufacturer, but that it would be a great benefit to the Canadian farmer, and that is the reason why the farmers in my riding supported me so strongly in the last election. They knew if anything came up in this House that would be to their benefit I would not fail them. ,
We have many serious problems, and one perhaps more serious than any other is that of our great railway system, with its 22,000 miles, with its annual deficit and the effect that has upon the whole country. Trade cherishes the railway as its best customer, buying thousands of tons of coal annually, using the steel and iron of many

The Budget-Mr. Low
mills, and the products of our vast forests, and giving employment to 185,000 men, providing a living for, at least, 900,000 of our population, and I am sure that anything that would affect our railways would affect the country. When the railways are depressed, the whole business of the country is depressed. Anything that will be for the benefit of our railways will be for the benefit of our country as a whole, as the deficits of the railways are paid by the people of this country.
Every proposed law that comes before this House should be scrutinized, because, after all, any blunders that are made are, in the last analysis, paid for by the people of the country. It is a strange coincidence that just 50 years ago the United States were passing through the same experience, and had the same problem to contend with that we have to-day. In the year 1872 President Grant, in his message to ongress, recommended that a select committee be appointed to investigate freight rates between the west and the east. The farmers of the western states at that time were groaning under the same burden that the farmers of the Canadian West are groaning under to-day, and, as a result of that investigation made by Congress, rates were reduced. I will read what history records 50 years ago.
The lower rates conceded to shippers induced an increase in the general volume of traffic. The farmers prospered beoause rates were reduced and the shareholders and the railway companies, who had not prospered hitherto themselves, realized that it was business and not high rates that they required in order to make money on their investments.
In that same year the commission reported, and one paragraph from the report reads as follows:
The cry of despair which comes from the overburdened west; the demand for cheaper food heard from the labouring classes of the east and from the plantations of the south, and the rapid falling off of our principal articles of export all indicate the imperative necessity for cheaper means of national transportation.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what the West needs to-day is cheaper freight rates. The importance of the railways to the West, I am sure, will be admitted by everybody, and it seems to me that they should have the lowest possible freight rates. What the seas are to England the railways are to our Canadian West. Without the railways the West would be in as bad a condition as England would be without the seas. The great problem in connection with our railways is, by what means shall cheap
and ample facilities be provided for the interchange of commodities between the different sections of our widely extended country? Everybody knows that the interior growth of any country is due to the railways. The demand of the people of the West to-day is for adequate and cheap transportation. We heard the Minister of Railways (Mr. Kennedy), when he addressed the House sometime ago, outline his proposals and, I think, if we are to succeed with our railways, it can only be done by giving the minister a free hand and a fair opportunity to operate those railways upon business principles and business methods. Sectional interests must igiive way to the larger interests of all the people. Increased business with the railways will reduce the deficits as well as lower the rates of the railway. As members from Ontario, we are deeply interested in railways, because, after all, the lion's share of the deficit will fall upon the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. We have heard many speakers, but after all, unless some constructive policy is suggested and adopted we will not accomplish anything. I believe that, if we are to wipe out our railway deficit, it can be done in one way and in one way only, and that is by increased population-an increased number of settlers upon the land.
I will endeavour to present to the House what, in my opinion, is the solution of some of our national ills and financial burdens. It has been said by eminent railway authorities that every settler placed upon the land is worth $746 annually to the railways. If that be the case, the first thing the Government should do is to inaugurate a progressive immigration policy. No doubt there is a certain class of immigrants we do not wish to see coming into the country, but there are people we would welcome. We should first make an attempt to reclaim many of the Canadian citizens who have gone to United States. How are we going to accomplish anything in the way ot immigration? We have 19 immigration agencies in the cities of the States and twelve agencies in the United Kingdom. I think the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Stewart) should waken up these agencies, rouse them, and treat them in the same way as a business man would treat one of his agencies. If a business man finds that a manager in his office in a foreign country is not doing any business, he wants to know the reason, and, if the business is not forthcoming, he will quickly make a
The Budget-Mr. Low

change. I believe that if every one of these thirty-one agencies was alive to the requirements of the country, we would see an influx of immigration that we have never had before.
We would like to see as many settlers from the United States as possible. They are very much like ourselves, and 1 believe they would settle our lands and make first-class citizens of this country. I believe an immigration policy should be put in effect in England that would induce as many as possible to come to this country. There is, in England, a class of people who, I believe, are available and possibly could be induced to come to this country, a class of educated, trained agriculturist families. English periodicals tell us that many of these families which, before the war, had sufficient incomes to maintain themselves in considerable affluence, find the inroads of the war and the pressing burden of taxation so great that they are unable to maintain their former standard of living and their financial position, and the capital realized from the sale of their lands and the income which is still theirs would enable members of this group to exist in a comfortable condition in this country. A determined and special campaign directed towards this group would result in bringing to Canada large numbers of permanent settlers of a most desirable type. In England and Scotland there are many young farmers who, by personal service during the war, have saved up sufficient means to purchase small land holdings. Many of these men have been agriculturists, gardeners, country merchants while their wives and sisters have been brought up in the country and in country villages and are accustomed to rural life. They, to my mind, would make most desirable settlers.
In Scandinavian countries, there is also a class of people who will make most desirable citizens, and I would refer more particularly in this category to Norwegians, Swedes, Danes and Icelanders. More Swedish farmers came to Canada from the United States than came from Sweden. The population of Sweden is not very large, but history tells us that those who have emigrated to the United States have made excellent citizens. According to the records, 43 per cent of those who emigrated to the United States have remained and are to-day on the land. Of eleven groups investigated, the Swedes committed fewer crimes than almost any other nationality. The Norwegians, like
fMr. Low.]
the other Scandinavian races, are a hardy adventurous race, and they become naturalized citizens very quickly. They have sent to the United States more people than almost any other nation except the Irish, and there are nearly one-half as many Norwegians in the United States as there t are in Norway. We might very properly turn our attention to this class of immigration. An investigation of Norwegians in the United States revealed the fact that 63 per cent of them were engaged in agriculture, and I am sure that what we require in the settler coming into this country is that he will settle upon the land. More than one-third of the Norwegian farmers in the United States are settled in Minnesota, one-fifth in Wisconsin, and the production of those two states in wheat and other farm products, as well as the general development, speak well for the type of settlers and citizens they make. I might go on at some length; but I believe if a businesslike immigration policy is introduced in this country, it will do more to relieve the deficits of our railways than any other method that we can adopt.
I am not going to detain the House longer; I merely wish to -say, in conclusion, that we have a great country; but we can only keep it great provided all our people are united and contented. That, Mr. Speaker, above all else, should be the guiding star and the aim of every .administration, so that every shade of thought is duly considered in the framing of policies and in the carrying out of those policies. Liberal administrations have adhered to those principles in the past; and if the present Liberal Government lives up to the traditions of the great Liberal party, we may look forward to the dawn of a new era of prosperity, contentment and happiness.
