subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as this is the first time I have

The Budget-Mr. IV. Black
spoken, I have a considerable feeling of diffidence in the presence of the many old parliamentarians whom I see around me and who have been in this House for so long a time. I must at the outset confess that I have been rather disappointed in the budget that has been brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). In the election of 1921, the Liberals, when they came out to oppose us, told us that the two parties were practically the same, but I differ greatly with that statement as I take my stand in the House. Last fall at Calgary the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) delivered an address in which he spoke about the downward revision of the tariff and also a complete elimination of those duties which we have had for many years; but there is surely something radically wrong when we compare those statements with what we find in the budget that has been brought down by the Minister of Finance. This reminds me of an address that the ex-President of the United States made about a year ago, when he stated that he had never seen a minister of finance deliver a budget speech without a joker at the end of it. Had farm implements been left as they were instead of a reduction of 2i per cent being made in the duty and then there being added, as it were, as the ex-President of the United States said, two or three jokers, I would have been quite well satisfied, especially if my hon. friend had put an excise tax on all those articles that are manufactured in this country.
The minister speaks as though it were a difficult undertaking to raise the revenue. Our good friends to our right almost declare that unless there is high protection, you cannot manufacture goods in this country. If they want high protection, I would advocate the imposition of an excise tax, and then some of the money will go into the treasury of this country instead of all going into the pockets of the manufacturers.
Let us consider some of these manufactured goods. In the first place, I think we could easily reduce the duty on boots and shoes by one-half. And let me say right here that the boots and shoes that have been manufactured in Canada during the past six or eight years have been .hardly fit for any man or woman to wear. I have known instances where children's boots, costing between $3 or $4 per pair, coming out of the factories here, have gone to pieces after three weeks of wear. The manufacturers of these particular articles should, I think, use more brains and better
material in making them, because the class of goods they turn out at present is certainly not a credit to them. As one hon. gentleman near me suggests, they should put more leather and less paper in them, and there is a good deal of truth in that. In the year 1921, there were imported into this country over $2,000,000 worth of boots and shoes, while the exports totalled over $1,500,000. Of these exports some $354,000 worth went across the border. Now, if these manufacturers can compete with the American manufacturers, sending this quantity of boots into the United States, I think they should certainly be able to meet the competition of the boots exported from the United States into Canada. The exports of boots and shoes from Canada to Great Britain in the same period amounted to $904,000.
I think the Minister of Finance should have given more consideration to the question of building materials and agricultural implements. I have been informed on good authority, and the fact was mentioned in the House yesterday, that the manufacturers' warehouses are filled to the roofs with farm implements, and I understand that the same thing is true in regard to other manufactured goods that are used in building in this country. If these gentlemen would only lower their prices, as the farmers have done, this Dominion to-day would not be in the condition which is so generally deplored, and there would not be so many men walking the streets, because people would be able to buy and money would be in circulation. I know that the common talk in my part of the country is this: "We will not buy implements until these men decide to bring down their prices". That is the attitude of the people in western Ontario, and I for one do not blame them. If these men keep their manufactured products in the warehouses in the hope of being able to sell them at exorbitant prices, where are the farmers going to stand?
There is a further consideration in regard to the manufacturers in Canada. They are given a rebate on the duty they pay on raw material entering into the manufacture of goods which they ship out of the country. I contend that this is unreasonable, because I think that they can compete with the manufacturers across the line, or with those of any other country.
There is a good deal of talk about the want of population in Canada, but I do not see how we can hope to increase our
The Budget-Mr. W. Black

papulation or retain the people we have already, unless we can improve conditions and make the country more attractive to intending immigrants. In the last decade, taking the natural increase with the immigration that came into the country, our population ought to have been 11,000,000, and it is quite obvious that conditions in Canada could not have been such as to appeal to the people who left. When the hon. member who spoke a few moments ago (Mr. Low) said that 73 per cent of the produce of this country was consumed in Canada, I was almost staggered. That may be true, and I am not going to doubt the hon. gentleman's word but I can hardly credit the fact.
I do not want to take up much time, but I desire briefly to refer to the railway situation. Let me tell the Minister of Railways (Mr. Kennedy) at once that as a good Canadian I believe that the National Railways can be operated and made to pay inside of three years, provided the right men are placed at the head of the system. I might as well express the opinion here as in the back concessions of my constituency, and I will tell the minister that the sooner he changes the management of the railways the better it will be for them. He must begin a vigorous use of the pruning knife, and most of all he must have at the head of the railways a man in whom the people can -have the fullest confidence. No one has any faith in the man who is to-day at the head of the railways. That is the common view all over the western part of Ontario, and the sooner the minister gets a young man with a broad vision, who has his name to make, and places him in charge, the sooner will the National Railways be made to pay for themselves.
I might go on to speak of the merchant marine, but as the time is short I shall not do so. I should like, however, to say a word or two about the Civil Service. I think the service is over-manned, and I was about to suggest that it could be reduced by one-third. At all events, I do not think there is any doubt about the fact that it could be curtailed to advantage. But if I mistake not, there will be as many civil servants in Ottawa at the end of this year as at the beginning. In my opinion the civil servants could be reduced by thousands, and I would ask the Government seriously to get down to business in that direction and see that the service is cut down where-ever there is over-manning. Any minister, if he goes through his own department, can, I believe, find instances of this.

There is one other matter I shall refer to before concluding; but in passing I might suggest that a good deal of time has been wasted during the past week in this debate. I think that the man who talks for over half an hour, apart from the leaders of the parties and their lieutenants, is taking up too much time. However, to proceed. Our hon. friend the Minister of Finance visited Washington some time ago, and we often hear it said -that he might as well have stayed at home. Now, I do not agree with that, for I believe in dealing with our first cousins across the line, if I might so describe them. The United States is our best market and probably always will be. Just to spend a few moments on the question of our trade relations with that country, I might refer to the reciprocity treaty of 1854. Under that treaty Canada's exports to the United States increased from $10,750,000 in 1854, to almost $38,000,000 in 1866. Twenty years later, in 1886, our exports to the United States were only $34,000,000. Our exports nearly quadrupled in twelve years of reciprocity. In twenty years, when comparatively mild tariff restrictions existed, they declined by $3,500,000. Later on, when real restrictions began with the McKinley tariff, the effect was more injurious and was felt by the farmers of Canada with particular force. In 1888 Canada's export of animals and their products to the United States amounted to $7,500,000. In the fiscal year of 1893, when the McKinley tariff had made its full effect felt, they were down to less than $4,000,000. In the same period our exports of other products of agriculture shrank from $10,000,000 to $4,000,000. About that time occurred the darkest period in the whole agricultural history of Canada. Potatoes were sold on the Toronto market at 20 cents and 25 cents per bag, while good cattle in the country sold for from $12 to $15 per head. The only wonder was that farmers were able to exist at all. A great many of them left their farms, and a great deal of the best blood of rural Ontario emigrated to the United States during the dark days of the early nineties.
The first relief came in 1897, not with any easing up of the American tariff but merely as a result of the removal of quarantine regulations. About the year 1891 there had been a ninety-day quarantine against cattle moving either way across the border. Hon. Mr. Fisher, when he became federal Minister of Agriculture, se-

The Budget-Mr. Lovie
cured the removal of that obstruction, and as a direct result, although the American tariff still remained, our exports of cattle across the border jumped from 1,646 head in 1896 to 90,000 head two years later. The effect was immediate, prices beginning at once to advance with the removal of the quarantine. And still we hear people saying that the market across the line will hold up our own market here. Well, our own market is good enough, but still we have a surplus to export, and the American market is the best market we have.
The real boom came, however, in 1913, when some agricultural products were placed on the United States free list, and duties in all lines were greatly reduced. As a result our exports of cattle alone to the United States during the seven years from 1914 to 1920, inclusive, averaged 260,000 head per year, as against 28,000 head in 1913. Our exports of all animals and the products of animals advanced from less than $13,000,000 in 1913 to $113,000,000 in 1920. Our exports of other agricultural products went up from $27,000,000 to $52,000,000 at the same time, our fisheries advanced from $5,750,000 to $18,500,000, and our forest products from less than $30,000,000 to $71,000,000. All told, there was an increase in our exports to the United States in all lines in eight years from less than $140,000,000 to $464,000,0000. If any stronger argument is required as to the value of the American market for Canadian producers, Mr. Speaker, I should like our good friends to the right of us to let us know about it.
The last American tariff went into force on the 28th May, 1921. In the first six months after that tariff was introduced our exports of wool to the United States amounted to only $13,560, as compared with nearly $1,000,000 for the same period in the previous year. Our export of potatoes was only $447,000 in the firsit six months after the new tariff came into force, as compared with $2,000,000 in the same period of 1920. , Milk exports were less than $200,000 during 1921, while they were $1,295,000 in the previous year; our sheep exports were $421,000 as against $1,500,000; our cattle $2,369,000 compared with $17,000,000.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am entirely in accord with the sentiments of the last speaker (Mr. Low) in regard to immigration. I believe our own Canadian boys are worth two or three of any class of immigrants that we can bring in. I think the Minister
of Immigration would do well to try and get as many as possible of our Canadian men to come back from the States, instead of encouraging too many immigrants from the Old Land. We need immigration to solve our railway problem, but at the present time I am strongly against spending so much money to bring in immigrants until we are able to hold the people we have here.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, In rising to take part in this debate, I wish, along with those who have already spoken, to extend to the hon. Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) congratulations upon his sixteenth budget speech in the Canadian Parliament. It is a unique record for a finance minister in any country, and one which it is very hard to duplicate. I give the hon. minister credit for all the reductions he has made upon foodstuffs and agricultural implements, but I would say that in my humble opinion, and looking at the proposition from the viewpoint of a western farmer, these reductions do not begin to go far enough to remove the handicaps under which agriculture, the basic industry of Canada, is suffering and has been suffering for the past forty years, ever since the inauguration of the national policy.
Of course we know that revenue has to be raised, and that it is the finance minister's first duty to provide money to run the affairs of the country, but a tariff that will impose handicaps upon the principal industry of the country is, in my judgment, not the best sort of encouragement to hand out to that industry, and expect it to be prosperous and develop and show life. The farmer is in the unique position of having

The Budget-Mr. Lovie

to pay whatever tax is imposed upon him as there is no one to whom he can transfer it. A manufacturer passes on the tariff tax he has paid to the wholesaler, who in turn passes the same with a profit to the retailer, who also in turn adds the whole thing together, and the consumer-the farmer- pays it. It ends there as there is no one he can pass the tax on to.
Were a customs tariff framed with the avowed object of raising revenue-suppose nothing else were in the finance minister's mind-then all the money collected under that tariff would go into the Dominion treasury and be available to pay the expenses of the country. But such is not the case. Under a protective tariff as we have had it in Canada, the Canadian manufacturer pockets the amount of customs duties and as the farmer has to pay them he is to that extent less able to pay into the national finances. Customs taxes place money in the federal treasury only when they are paid to the customs house officers at the regular ports of entry. But, Mr. Speaker, I contend it is not fair that anyone should be entitled, whether he be manufacturer or agriculturist, to put money into his pocket that really should belong either to the consumer or to the Dominion treasury.
A protective tariff was first inaugurated in Canada forty years ago to boost the manufacturing interests, and boost them it certainly did, until they were top-heavy. It made them act not as though they were giving service to the country as a whole, but as if they were the whole country. In the natural and successful development of a country the logical idea would be first to find the principal industry of that country, what the country was best adapted to, and then develop that industry. It is conceded by all that agriculture is the basic industry of Canada, and that being the case, it needs encouragement. So far in the history of Canada it has not had encouragement; it has really been poverty stricken. Let anyone examine the wage schedules of any competing agency for workingmen, whether in the case of manufacturers, the railways, the professions-in fact, any concern that employs men, and invariably you will find these firms offering larger remuneration than the farmer can afford to pay; consequently, the best men leave the farms.
Were manufactures to be developed as a secondary industry with a view 11 p.m. to supplying the needs of the consumers at a reasonable cost

and to selling the balance of their output in the open markets of the world, things would be different. But what is the state of affairs to-day? We find that implements are sold to the Canadian farmer by the Canadian manufacturer at a profit on the cost of production and then the customs duty added to that, while at the same time the Canadian manufacturer goes to other countries and sells that same machine far cheaper than he sells it to his home consumer. In proof of this I will give you a concrete example.
As the conditions of agriculture in the three prairie provinces correspond in a large measure with the conditions in the states to the south just across the international boundary as far as soil and climate are concerned, we in western Canada claim that to put the farming industry of Canada on an equal footing with the industry just across the boundary, and so enable us to keep the native born Canadian at home-and also to keep the immigrant who comes to our shores to develop agriculture in Canada, and incidentally to make a home and a competence for himself-we need to get our agricultural implements as cheaply as possible.
It was generally conceded at the last general election, and is just as necessary now as then-more so, in fact, because at election time these were only suggestions; now they are far more than that-that five things were absolutely necessary, to lift agriculture out of the mud and mire in which it had found itself placed, and set it upon a higher plane. These were: Reduc-ion in the tariff; reduction in freight rates; cheap agricultural implements; wider markets; a better system of marketing our wheat.
Reduction in the customs tariff I have already spoken about. The pre-war period was not a prosperous time for agriculture. Agriculture was not on a par with other industries, and consequently languished. There are ir. western Canada millions of acres of as fertile soil as ever the sun shone upon, waiting for men and women to work and develop it, but at present no one who is not already engaged in farming will undertake such a proposition. Conditions have been worse for the farmer at this period of depression than at any other period, because the purchasing power of the dollar has been very low. The price of wheat went down as much in one year after the last war as it did in six years after the American civil war, and went down further. Mr. John Bracken, presi-

The Budget-Mr. Lovie
dent of the Manitoba Agricultural College, at the convention of agricultural societies held in Winnipeg in January of this year, stated that the American government had set aside one thousand million dollars to assist in financing farming operations in their country in 1922, and that their farmers had advantages which ours did not enjoy.
As rigid economy must be practised in handling the finances of the country, I would suggest to the Minister of Finance that he let the agricultural implements of the country carry as light a load of taxation as possible so as to give encouragement to the industry of agriculture, because if it is prosperous, all others will be prosperous in turn. Business men by the dozen said to me last fall, "The farmers are good spenders. If they have money, I will have money too, but if they have no money there is none for me and as they get theirs from the soil there is no one they can fall back upon." I am talking about a purely agricultural country; the money comes from the soil, and when the crop fails there is nothing else for the farmer to fall back upon.
Of course, there are other difficulties the farmers have to contend with as well as the injustices of a protective tariff; but the federal government have it absolutely within their power tc remedy the injustices arising out of a protective tariff. A protective tariff is not a popular doctrine to preach in any of the three prairie provinces, where the people are situated a long way from markets and pay high transportation costs on all they ship out and all they bring in. They need every encouragement possible in the way of removing handicaps to their industry. I would suggest again that if it is absolutely necessary for revenue purposes to keep a tariff tax upon agricultural implements, a corresponding tax for revenue purposes be placed upon all implements of home manufacture.
Reduction in freight rates is very important, but there will be an opportunity to discuss that later when the bill with respect to the matter is before the House.
A better system of marketing our wheat is necessary in the national interest, but this also will be before the House, so need not be taken up now. I would just like to emphasize what has been already said, that no one whc is not actively engaged in farming really believes, even if he pretends to believe, that the granting of a
national marketing agency with compulsory powers to handle the wheat of the country, is protection as it is generally understood. If it is, I for one am quite willing for the finance department to collect from me every dollar the wheat board pays me for wheat, over and above what the world markets warrant, less storage and transportation charges. The idea of a wheat board is to cut out the big slump in prices that occurs as soon as the movement of the wheat starts in the fall, to hold the market steady, and to see that the producer gets for his wheat all that the world's markets warrant.
As the development of the natural resources is the first and most important industry in Canada, and as the greatest of all natural resources in western Canada is the top six inches of fertile soil, so one of the prime requisites of that part of the Dominion is to have some place to sell its products outside of our own country. It is the function of provincial legislatures to look after the domestic affairs of the different provinces, but finding export markets is something that comes purely within the scope of the Dominion Parliament. A large percentage of the farmers of the three prairie provinces feel very sore over the loss of the market to the south just across the boundary line. True, we have no say in that at present, but if we cast our eyes back to the general election of 1911, we do not need long distance field glasses to discern what particular political party worked hard and successfully to shut the Canadian farmer out from the market to the south, and to-day that same party openly avow upon the floor of the House that they are in favour of restricted markets. I claim, Mr. Speaker, that had there been reciprocity in natural products between the two great countries- Canada and the United States-from 1911 up to the spring of 1921, the advantages to both would have been so apparent that no endeavour would have been made to interfere with the free flow of natural products north and south.
Canada, in effect, said to the United States in 1911, just exactly what the campaign cry meant, "No truck or trade with the Yankees." And the Yankees have certainly taken us at our word now, but Mr. Speaker, I commend the action of the Finance Minister, at the beginning of this session in making an endeavour to secure better trade relations with our neighbours to the south. I wish him God speed on

The Budget-Mr. Lovie
that undertaking and I would heartily commend to the notice of the Government and the House the recommendation of my worthy leader, the hon. member from Marquette (Mr. Crerar), that Canada should have representation at Washington.
From 1917 until the spring of 1921 livestock had free access to the American market, but when the Fordney tariff took effect, it seemed as if a cyclone had struck the Canadian livestock interests. The two greatest livestock marketing centres in Canada are the cities of Winnipeg and Toronto. What is the effect of the Fordney tariff upon these markets? The livestock shipper from my district in Manitoba told me personally last fall, that he saw nothing for it but to pay duty and ship his cattle to Chicago, as the Winnipeg market was so congested that one carload of cattle would knock it endways.
About the Toronto market I know nothing personally, but I can give the evidence of a gentleman living within twenty-five miles of Ottawa who has handled thousands of cattle in Ontario, and who has assured me since I came to Ottawa, that he was entirely out of the cattle shipping business since the market to the south was cut off because he could sell fifteen carloads of cattle in Buffalo just as easily as he could sell two head in Toronto. Since coming to Ottawa I have learned on the floor of the House that the maritime provinces depend very largely on the market in the United States directly south of them for the sale of their potato crop. Mr. W. A. Brown of the Poultry Division, Ottawa, speaking at the Agricultural Society's Convention in Winnipeg in the spring of this year, said:
We need to look for wider markets than we have at present for poultry products. We want to see Canada shipping poultry products to the great cities of Boston, New York and Philadelphia, just the same as they ship to us, oranges, lemons and walnuts. Thirty-flve carloads of poultry were shipped, live weight, from Prince Edward Island last year to Boston, 3,000 birds to a car, and 16,000 carloads of fowl were consumed by the Jews in New York alone last year.
Coming to Ontario, I find that the district in the southern part of the province lying along the shore of Lake Erie, has become properous growing garden and field truck for the United States market. The city of Detroit with a population of over 1,000,000 is within easy reach of that district; it sends motor trucks into the fields where the produce is grown and takes it into Detroit, paying duty on it. The

northern part of the state of Michigan being rocky and bushy, no truck is raised there, and Detroit depends on the southern part of Ontario for a large part of the necessaries of life, and the Ontario farmers are only too pleased to supply them. Farther west, some of the farmers are raising Kubanka wheat. There are no mills in Canada to grind Kubanka wheat. No mills nearer than Minneapolis can do so. Being practically rust resistant, Kubanka does better than Marquis in a year when rust bothers the crop. But the restricted markets which we have at present are against the raising of this particular kind of wheat.
I did want to say a word or two about freight rates, but that subject will come up later in the House. However, I would just like to mention one instance as to how freight rates are killing the trade of this country. An Ontario farmer was in our district last fall during threshing time, and wanted to take a car load of potatoes from Manitoba to his home district, because there was a scarcity of potatoes there. He could get potatoes at 70 cents a bushel f.o.b. the car. He found, however, that the freight was $1 a bushel so it was prohibitive to ship them; the producer would get 70 cents for his potatoes but it would take $1 a bushel to ship them to their destination. In that case there was nothing doing, and that is one of the reasons why farming is getting so unprofitable. There are many other similar instances that could be cited.
, I submit, Mr. Speaker, that western farmers are not kicking against existing conditions without reason. I would like to draw the attention of the House to one of the statements made by Mr. Sanford Evans while giving evidence before the Committee on Agriculture on the subject of the " Wheat Board." He said that those who cannot make money out of wheat raising at present prices have no business to be raising wheat, and that, in spite of the fact that wheat prices had fallen below cost of production. Mr. Sanford Evans also said at the same time that the price of all commodities the farmer had to purchase had started to come down before the price of farm produce came down. What are the facts? In the fall of 1920 wheat prices came down a half and stayed down. In March of 1921 the manufacturers and implement dealers of western Canada in convention assembled, decided that the price of farm implements was not high enough and raised the price 30 per cent. The blacksmiths of Mani-

The Budget-Mr. Lovie
toba at the same time met in annual convention and raised their prices 25 per cent, and this in spite of the fact that prices of farm produce were cut in two. These men certainly showed that they hated to take a loss.
It comes hard to give up money that people thought they had made, some honestly and some by outrageous profiteering, out of the world's dire extremity; but it must be disgorged just the same.
We are not to see that equilibrium, without which there can be no widespread resumption of business, until every mother's son of us shall have let go of all the temporary advantages gained under the stress of feverish war activities. They were all unfair, unreasonable and uneconomic at the time. They represented not honest reward nor effort, but a world's agony. They could have no permanent place in any man's industrial or business calculation.
Will people never learn the lesson that we are absolutely interdependent. It seems not. The starting point of the prosperity of every man, woman and child in Canada is a living wage for the farmer. The western farmer who has to take 18 or 20 cents a bushel for his oats is in no position to buy merchandise or machinery made and transported by labour receiving the price of 20 to 50 bushels of oats per day. That fact is so plain, that any wage arbitrator or price-fixing conference should understand it.
We have more respect for plain everyday highwaymen than we have for those who have not yet relinquished ill-gotten gains and accepted their losses. Of course, we hate to take a loss, even though it be a mere return of money which we thought had come to us as a blessing from heaven while Germany sat on our neck; but it came from the hell of war and1 we have no business trying to hang on to it any longer at the expense of barring the return of general business activity. The sooner the war booty is turned into the common pool, the sooner all will again find incomes equal to necessary expenditures.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have not offered any remedy for the loss of revenue likely to come to the treasury through the lowering of the tariff on agricultural implements, which I have suggested. If the farmer were in a better position financially he would be in a better position to pay income taxes, something which he is
not able to do at present to any great extent as he has not the income. There are a few suggestions in the Farmers' platform issued by the Canadian Council of Agriculture in 1918 which I would commend to the notice of the Minister of Finance.
The farmers in my neighbourhood paid income tax pretty considerab.y in 1920, but, on the 1921 crop, I am afraid there will be very little income tax paid.
There is a system of collecting revenue, which I am going to bring to the notice of the Finance Minister, and the members of this House, of which I do not approve, and I would like an expression of opinion from the Finance Minister as to whether or not he approves of it, or how much of it has been done. I may say that the Income Tax Department are penalizing religious institutions. I do not know that it would be well to bring out the facts, but I would like to place them before the minister sometime or other. I have an idea that religious organizations were exempt from taxation, but I have a proof in my pocket that they are not.
